Do Neural Models Prefer Their Submodels?

 

Álvaro Ribot          Yulia Alexandr          Anna Seigal

Harvard University          University of Melbourne          Harvard University

Abstract

A neural model is the set of functions that can be expressed by a given neural network architecture. Neural models contain natural submodels, such as those obtained by setting some neurons to be inactive. We study the geometry of neural models and ask whether they prefer their submodels. By this we mean whether local minimizers of the loss function lie in a given submodel. We introduce a geometric framework to determine if this occurs. For shallow multilayer perceptrons, we show that subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are never preferred. For deep multilayer perceptrons, we give conditions under which subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are not preferred. For lightning self-attention, lower-rank submodels are usually not preferred, but we identify examples where they are because they lie on a boundary of the model. Our results show that, aside from a few exceptions, preference for submodels cannot be explained by the geometry of the neural model, and must instead come from other sources such as training dynamics.

1 Introduction

A neural model ℱ\mathcal{F} is the set of functions that can be expressed by a given neural network architecture. Given a target function hh, we seek a minimizer of the distance function from hh to ℱ\mathcal{F}. Submodels are subsets of ℱ\mathcal{F} obtained by reducing hyperparameters, such as rank, or by requiring some neurons to be inactive. We study whether neural models prefer their submodels or, more specifically, whether a local minimizer of the distance from hh to ℱ\mathcal{F} lies in a given submodel ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. We call this behavior proximity bias.

Training a model is known to produce solutions that lie on, or close to, one of these submodels (Frankle and Carbin, 2019; Arora et al., 2019; Shahverdi et al., 2026). This could be due to structure in the data, the optimization dynamics, loss function, or the geometry of the neural model. Identifying why it occurs is important to understand how models generalize and how to change their behavior. We seek to isolate the role of the neural model geometry, which affects the dynamics and loss in a downstream way.

Compared to general points in a given model, points on submodels may possess more tangent directions to the model or fewer. Proximity bias can occur only in the latter case, since a minimizer must lie in the polar of the tangent cone. We show that proximity bias is governed by the local geometry of the model along its submodel. Figure 1 illustrates our result for shallow MLPs: the submodel obtained using inactive hidden neurons has more tangent directions than a general point, so proximity bias does not occur.

Low-rank matrix approximation sets the scene. The best rank-at-most-rr approximation of a matrix MM in (e.g.) Frobenius norm has rank exactly rr, unless rank⁡(M)<r\operatorname{rank}(M)<r, due to Eckart and Young (1936). That is, a low-rank matrix model uses available degrees of freedom rather than collapsing to an even-lower-rank submodel. The analogous statement holds for symmetric tensors (Seigal and Sturmfels, 2017). This implies no proximity bias for single-output shallow MLPs with monomial activations. We extend this to deep MLPs and those with analytic activation functions, and to lightning self-attention.

1.1 Summary of contributions

We study two classes of neural models (also known as neuromanifolds): those corresponding to multilayer perceptrons and to lightning self-attention. For shallow MLPs, we show that the narrower submodel obtained by removing a hidden neuron is not preferred. For deep MLPs, inactive neurons are again not preferred in several cases: when one neuron is inactive in every hidden layer, when the earlier layers are wide enough, when the activations are polynomial of sufficiently high degree, and when the activations are analytic but not polynomial. For attention, many lower-rank and singular strata do not exhibit proximity bias, but certain exceptional singular or boundary strata do. We show that singularity alone does not determine whether a submodel is preferred; it is governed by a finer geometry of the neural model; see Figure 2 for examples.

1.2 Related work

Implicit and sparsity bias.

Trained models have been shown to prefer structured solutions, such as max-margin, low-rank or sparse ones, without them appearing in the objective function. This phenomenon is called implicit bias (Soudry et al., 2018; Gunasekar et al., 2017; Gunasekar et al., 2018; Chizat and Bach, 2020). A preference for networks with fewer active neurons is called sparsity bias: the noise of stochastic gradient descent drives networks toward simpler subnetworks (Chen et al., 2023), and randomly initialized networks contain small subnetworks that perform comparably when trained alone (Frankle and Carbin, 2019). Other works trace a preference for simple functions to the architecture or the parametrization (Valle-Pérez et al., 2019; Mingard et al., 2025). Our notion of proximity bias depends only on the geometry of the neural model and is one possible source of implicit bias.

Singularities and learning.

Singular learning theory studies models, including neural networks, that are not identifiable and whose Fisher information matrix is degenerate (Watanabe, 2009; Wei et al., 2022). Such singularities can cause plateaus in gradient-based learning (Amari et al., 2006), although these effects do not imply that singular points are local minimizers. These are singularities of the parametrization. We instead consider singularities and boundaries of the neural model itself, in the spirit of neuroalgebraic geometry (Marchetti et al., 2025), and our descriptions of neural models build on Kileel et al. (2019); Kubjas et al. (2024); Henry et al. (2025); Grosdos et al. (2025); Alexandr et al. (2026).

Subnetworks and critical points.

Two recent works connect sparsity bias to singularities. Shahverdi et al. (2026) study polynomial MLPs and show that, under mild conditions, subnetworks are singular points of the neural model and are critical points of the loss for an open set of targets. Kohn et al. (2026) study deep monomial networks of high degree and show that the parametrization is critical exactly at subnetworks. However, critical points may be saddles. We ask when these submodels contain local minima for an open set of targets.

2 Proximity bias

We introduce a geometric framework to study the presence or absence of proximity bias toward submodels. A neural model ℱ\mathcal{F} is a subset of a real Hilbert space of functions ℋ\mathcal{H}. For a fixed target function h∈ℋh\!\in\!\mathcal{H}, we consider the squared distance

ℓh:ℋ→ℝ,f↦ℓh​(f)=‖h−f‖2.\ell_{h}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R},f\mapsto\ell_{h}(f)=\|h-f\|^{2}.

We ask whether minimizing ℓh\ell_{h} over ℱ\mathcal{F} selects a distinguished lower-dimensional submodel ℱ′⊂ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{F}. Such a preference cannot arise through smooth interior points of ℱ\mathcal{F}; it can only occur where the local real geometry is nongeneric, for example along singular or boundary strata; see Proposition 2.4. One may think of the target function h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} as an oracle that best explains the data, or as a teacher from which we try to distill knowledge using students in ℱ\mathcal{F} (Hinton et al., 2015).

The Voronoi cell (Cifuentes et al., 2022) of f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} is

Vorℱ⁡(f)\displaystyle\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(f) ={h∈ℋ:‖h−f‖≤‖h−g‖​ for all ​g∈ℱ}\displaystyle=\{h\in\mathcal{H}:\|h-f\|\leq\|h-g\|\text{ for all }g\in\mathcal{F}\}
={h∈ℋ:f is a global minimizer of ℓh|ℱ}.\displaystyle=\{h\in\mathcal{H}:f\text{ is a global minimizer of }\ell_{h}\rvert_{\mathcal{F}}\}.

We introduce the local Voronoi cell of f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} as

Vorℱloc(f)={h∈ℋ:f is a local minimizer of ℓh|ℱ}.\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(f)=\{h\in\mathcal{H}:f\text{ is a local minimizer of }\ell_{h}\rvert_{\mathcal{F}}\}.

More generally, given a set ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}, we define its Voronoi cell and local Voronoi cell, respectively, as

Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=⋃f∈ℱ′Vorℱ⁡(f),Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=⋃f∈ℱ′Vorℱloc⁡(f).\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\!\!\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\!\!\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(f),\quad\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\!\!\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\!\!\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(f).

We say that ℱ\mathcal{F} exhibits proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} if Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) has nonempty interior in ℋ\mathcal{H}. When ℋ\mathcal{H} is finite-dimensional and ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} are semialgebraic sets (e.g., for polynomial neural networks), the set Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) is semialgebraic and the following are equivalent: Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) has nonempty interior in ℋ\mathcal{H}; Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) has a positive Lebesgue measure; dimVorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=dimℋ\dim\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\dim\mathcal{H}.

Remark 2.1.

Voronoi cells are closed convex sets that tessellate the ambient space. Local Voronoi cells are also convex, but may not be closed and may overlap.

We study (local) Voronoi cells using classical notions from variational geometry (Rockafellar and Wets, 1998). Tangent cones and their polar normal cones encode the first-order geometry relevant to local optimality; see Figure 2. Given f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, the tangent cone of ℱ\mathcal{F} at ff, denoted Tℱ​(f)T_{\mathcal{F}}(f), is the set of directions that arise as limits of sequences in ℱ\mathcal{F} tending to ff. In symbols,

Tℱ​(f)={v∈ℋ:∃(fn)n⊂ℱ,∃(τn)n⊂ℝ>0fn→f,(fn−f)/τn→v}.T_{\mathcal{F}}(f)=\left\{v\in\mathcal{H}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists(f_{n})_{n}\subset\mathcal{F},\;\exists(\tau_{n})_{n}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}\\ f_{n}\to f,\;(f_{n}-f)/\tau_{n}\to v\end{array}\right\}.

The normal cone of ℱ\mathcal{F} at ff is the polar cone of Tℱ​(f)T_{\mathcal{F}}(f):

Nℱ​(f)={w∈ℋ:⟨v,w⟩≤0​ for all ​v∈Tℱ​(f)}.N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)=\{w\in\mathcal{H}:\langle v,w\rangle\leq 0\text{ for all }v\in T_{\mathcal{F}}(f)\}.

When ff is a smooth point of ℱ\mathcal{F}, we recover the classical notions of tangent and normal spaces. The following chain of inclusions relates these sets.

Proposition 2.2.

Given any ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} one has

ℱ′⊆Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)⊆Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)⊆⋃f∈ℱ′(f+Nℱ​(f)).\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})\subseteq\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})\subseteq\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\bigl(f+N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)\bigr).
Proof idea.

The first inclusion follows from ℓf​(f)=0\ell_{f}(f)=0 and ℓf≥0\ell_{f}\geq 0. The second inclusion says that global minimizers are local minimizers. The third uses that −∇ℓh​(f)=2​(h−f)-\nabla\ell_{h}(f)=2(h-f) and that this vector lies in Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f) if ff is a local minimizer of ℓh|ℱ\ell_{h}\rvert_{\mathcal{F}}. See Appendix A. ∎

The above result uses the specificity of the normal cone to minimizers rather than any critical point.

Corollary 2.3.

If ⋃f∈ℱ′(f+Nℱ​(f))\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\bigl(f+N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)\bigr) has empty interior, then there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. If Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) has nonempty interior, then there is proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

There is always proximity bias toward equal-dimensional submodels and proximity bias toward a lower-dimensional submodel requires points where the normal cone is larger than at smooth points.

Proposition 2.4.

Assume dimℋ<∞\dim\mathcal{H}<\infty and consider semialgebraic sets ℱ′⊆ℱ⊆ℋ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{H}. If dimℱ′=dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{F}, then there is proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. If dimℱ′<dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\dim\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is contained in the smooth locus of ℱ\mathcal{F}, then there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

First, a full-dimensional semialgebraic subset ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} of ℱ\mathcal{F} agrees with ℱ¯\overline{\mathcal{F}} near some f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, so every target close to ff has all its nearest points of ℱ\mathcal{F} in ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Second, local Voronoi cells of smooth points have dimension at most dimℋ−dimℱ<dimℋ−dimℱ′\dim\mathcal{H}-\dim\mathcal{F}<\dim\mathcal{H}-\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. ∎

Remark 2.5 (Other losses).

Our setting can be generalized to other nondegenerate losses: Fréchet differentiable functions ℓu:ℋ→ℝ≥0\ell_{u}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} such that ℓu​(u)=0\ell_{u}(u)\!=\!0 and ∇ℓu​(f)=0\nabla\ell_{u}(f)=0 if and only if f=uf=u. The squared distance ℓu​(f)=‖f−u‖2\ell_{u}(f)=\|f-u\|^{2} is a nondegenerate loss because ∇ℓu​(f)=2​(f−u)\nabla\ell_{u}(f)=2(f-u). If ℋ\mathcal{H} is a finite-dimensional space, then the mean-squared error (MSE) is a nondegenerate loss function provided that the dataset is sufficiently general and large enough (Kohn et al., 2022).

3 Multilayer Perceptrons

Figure 3 conveys the idea behind this section. It shows the cone of functions computed by a single neuron. An inactive neuron computes the zero function, which is the apex of the cone. An inactive neuron can be reactivated in every direction of the cone, so submodels with inactive neurons have many tangent directions and tend not to be preferred. For shallow networks, this idea suffices to show that there is no proximity bias toward subnetworks. For deep networks, one must also take into account how the upstream and downstream layers affect the tangent directions added by inactive neurons, which makes the analysis more challenging.

Definition 3.1.

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) with architecture 𝐝=(d0,…,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{L}) and activation functions 𝝆=(ρ1,…,ρL)\bm{\rho}=(\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{L}) is a map

f𝐖,𝐛=ρ~L∘AL∘⋯∘ρ~1∘A1:ℝd0→ℝdL,f_{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}}=\tilde{\rho}_{L}\circ A_{L}\circ\cdots\circ\tilde{\rho}_{1}\circ A_{1}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}},

where Ak​(x)=Wk​x+bkA_{k}(x)=W_{k}x+b_{k} with Wk∈ℝdk×dk−1W_{k}\in{\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{k-1}}}, bk∈ℝdkb_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, and ρ~k:ℝdk→ℝdk\tilde{\rho}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} applies a fixed function ρk:ℝ→ℝ\rho_{k}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} coordinatewise. The neural model ℱ\mathcal{F} of the MLP is the set of functions f𝐖,𝐛f_{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}} as the weight matrices 𝐖=(W1,…,WL)\mathbf{W}=(W_{1},\dots,W_{L}) and biases 𝐛=(b1,…,bL)\mathbf{b}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{L}) vary over ∏kℝdk×dk−1\prod_{k}\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{k-1}} and ∏kℝdk\prod_{k}\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, respectively. The hyperparameter LL is the number of layers. We say that an MLP is shallow if L=2L=2, and deep if L≥3L\geq 3.

For simplicity, we assume linear readouts; i.e., the last activation function ρL\rho_{L} is the identity map. This assumption is mild, since the last activation can be absorbed by the loss function: ℓh​(ρ∘f)=(ℓh∘ρ)​(f)\ell_{h}(\rho\circ f)=(\ell_{h}\circ\rho)(f). We assume that all other activations are nonconstant.

Given a fixed MLP architecture and activation functions, we take the ambient space ℋ\mathcal{H} of the neural model ℱ\mathcal{F} to be the completion of its linear span with respect to a fixed inner product: ℋ=span⁡(ℱ)¯\mathcal{H}=\overline{\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F})}. When all activations are polynomials, ℱ\mathcal{F} consists of (tuples of) polynomials of bounded degree, so ℋ\mathcal{H} is finite-dimensional and we take the standard inner product of polynomials (Bombieri inner product). When some activation is non-polynomial, the universal approximation theorem implies that span⁡(ℱ)\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F}) is infinite dimensional, and we take an L2L^{2} inner product with respect to a finite compactly-supported Borel measure μ\mu on ℝd0\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}, so that ℋ=span⁡(ℱ)¯=L2​(μ,ℝdL)\mathcal{H}=\overline{\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F})}=L^{2}(\mu,\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}}). This implies restricting the support of elements in ℱ\mathcal{F} to guarantee that their norm is finite. When the support of μ\mu is a finite set Ω\Omega, the functions in the restricted neural model ℱ|Ω\mathcal{F}|_{\Omega} are identified with vectors in ℝ|Ω|×dL\mathbb{R}^{|\Omega|\times d_{L}}, a finite-dimensional ambient space. Equipping ℝ|Ω|×dL\mathbb{R}^{|\Omega|\times d_{L}} with the Euclidean inner product corresponds to MSE for the dataset Ω\Omega.

3.1 Shallow Networks

Consider MLPs with architecture 𝐝=(d0,d1,d2)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},d_{1},d_{2}) and activations 𝝆=(ρ~,id)\bm{\rho}=(\tilde{\rho},\operatorname{id}). The single-neuron cone is

𝒞={f⁡(x)=ρ⁡(⟨w,x⟩+β)​v+b:w∈ℝd0,β∈ℝv,b∈ℝd2}.\mathcal{C}\!=\!\left\{f(x)=\rho(\langle w,x\rangle+\beta)v+b:\!\begin{array}[]{l}w\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}},\beta\in\mathbb{R}\\ v,b\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}\end{array}\!\!\right\}.

The single-neuron cone is the neural model of MLPs with architecture (d0,1,d2)(d_{0},1,d_{2}) and activations 𝝆=(ρ~,id)\bm{\rho}=(\tilde{\rho},\operatorname{id}): f⁡(x)f(x) above is f𝐖,𝐛f_{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}} with 𝐖=(w⊤,v)\mathbf{W}=(w^{\top},v) and 𝐛=(β,b)\mathbf{b}=(\beta,b).

Lemma 3.2.

The neural model ℱ\mathcal{F} of a shallow MLP with architecture (d0,d1,d2)(d_{0},d_{1},d_{2}) is the Minkowski sum of d1d_{1} single-neuron cones: ℱ=∑i=1d1𝒞.\mathcal{F}=\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{d_{1}}\mathcal{C}. Therefore, span⁡(𝒞)=span⁡(ℱ)\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{C})=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F}).

We think of nonzero elements in 𝒞\mathcal{C} as rank-one functions and elements in ℱ\mathcal{F} as rank at most d1d_{1} functions, by analogy to the following special case.

Example 3.3 (Symmetric matrices).

Consider the architecture 𝐝=(d0,d1,1)\mathbf{d}\!=\!(d_{0},d_{1},1) and 𝝆=(ρ~,id)\bm{\rho}=(\tilde{\rho},\operatorname{id}) with ρ⁡(t)=t2\rho(t)=t^{2}. The MLPs without bias terms (bk=0)(b_{k}=0) and weights 𝐖=(W,λ)\mathbf{W}=(W,\lambda) are quadratic forms

f𝐖,𝟎​(x)=x⊤​A​x,A=∑i=1d1λi​wi​wi⊤f_{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{0}}(x)=x^{\top}Ax,\quad A=\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{d_{1}}\lambda_{i}w_{i}w_{i}^{\top}

where wiw_{i} is the ii-th row of WW. Each hidden neuron contributes a rank-one term λi​wi​wi⊤\lambda_{i}w_{i}w_{i}^{\top}, so rank⁡A≤d1\operatorname{rank}A\leq d_{1}. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the set of d0×d0d_{0}\times d_{0} symmetric matrices of rank at most d1d_{1}, where d1<d0d_{1}<d_{0} and let ℱ′⊂ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{F} be its singular locus: points where the rank drops below d1d_{1}. As recalled above, the Eckart-Young theorem implies that a best rank-at-most-rr approximation of a matrix MM has rank rr (not smaller) unless rank⁡(M)<r\operatorname{rank}(M)<r. That is, Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Our next result extends this matrix example in three directions: to all local minimizers (not only global ones), to every inner product and nondegenerate loss, and to every activation function. Informally, we show that given a target function hh, a locally best rank-at-most-d1d_{1} approximation of hh has rank d1d_{1} (not smaller) unless rank⁡h<d1\operatorname{rank}h<d_{1}. See Figure 1.

Theorem 3.4.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of a shallow MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,d1,d2)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},d_{1},d_{2}), d1≥2d_{1}\geq 2, and activations (ρ~,id)(\tilde{\rho},\operatorname{id}). Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the closure of span⁡(ℱ)\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F}) with respect to a fixed inner product, and let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel with architecture 𝐝′=(d0,d1−1,d2)\mathbf{d}^{\prime}=(d_{0},d_{1}-1,d_{2}). Then,

Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′.\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

That is, a target function h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} admits a (local) minimizer of ℓh|ℱ\ell_{h}\rvert_{\mathcal{F}} in ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} if and only if h∈ℱ′h\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. The same holds with ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} replaced by their closures.

Proof idea.

We have ℱ′=∑i=1d1−1𝒞\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{1}-1}\mathcal{C} and ℱ=ℱ′+𝒞\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\mathcal{C}, by Lemma 3.2. Given any f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime} its tangent cone at ℱ\mathcal{F} contains 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which spans the whole ambient space. Hence, the normal cone Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f) is zero (see Figure 3) and the conclusion follows from Proposition 2.2. ∎

Details of all proofs in this section are in Appendix B, and details of all figures are in Appendix G.

Corollary 3.5.

Under the setup from Theorem 3.4, there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} whenever ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} has empty interior in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Thus, there is also no proximity bias toward (even) smaller subnetworks.

Remark 3.6 (Smallest Voronoi cells).

The equalities Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime} in Theorem 3.4 mean the cells are as small as possible, by Proposition 2.2.

Remark 3.7 (Saddle points in parameter space).

Our results pertain to function space, but have implications in parameter space. Inactive neurons (i.e., subnetworks) lead to critical points of the loss in parameter space for a nonempty open set of target functions (Kohn et al., 2026). Our tangent cone computation implies that these critical points cannot be local extrema at parameters where the parametrization is locally open (unless the loss vanishes there), so they must be saddle points.

Remark 3.8 (Bounding normal cones).

Conversely, results in parameter space can have implications in function space. Given a parametrization ϕ:Θ→ℱ\phi:\Theta\to\mathcal{F}, we have Nℱ(ϕ(θ))⊆im(dϕ|θ)⟂N_{\mathcal{F}}(\phi(\theta))\subseteq\operatorname{im}(d\phi\rvert_{\theta})^{\perp}, the orthogonal complement of the image of the differential of ϕ\phi at θ\theta. This containment can sometimes be used to deduce that there is no proximity bias, but not always (e.g. for MLPs) since we may have strict inequalities dimNℱ(ϕ(θ))<dimim(dϕ|θ)⟂\dim N_{\mathcal{F}}(\phi(\theta))<\dim\operatorname{im}(d\phi\rvert_{\theta})^{\perp}. In Appendix C we use this to show that there is no proximity bias toward subnetworks of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with polynomial activations.

3.2 Deep Networks

In this section, we consider deep MLPs. We start by analyzing proximity bias in the linear case.

Example 3.9 (Deep linear networks).

If all activations are the identity, the neural model of architecture (d0,…,dL)(d_{0},\dots,d_{L}) consists of affine maps ℝd0→ℝdL,x↦W​x+b\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}},x\mapsto Wx+b with rank⁡W≤r:=mink⁡dk\operatorname{rank}W\leq r:=\min_{k}d_{k}, so it is the neural model of the shallow linear network (d0,r,dL)(d_{0},r,d_{L}). If we remove a neuron from a bottleneck layer kk (i.e., one with dk=rd_{k}=r), there is no proximity bias toward the corresponding submodel, by Theorem 3.4. Otherwise, deleting a neuron of a hidden layer does not change the model (ℱ′=ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\mathcal{F}), so there is proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Unlike the shallow case, neural models of deep MLPs can no longer be expressed as a sum of single-neuron cones, in general. However, for some neural submodels ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} we can find a cone 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} whose span is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H} such that ℱ′+𝒞~⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{F}. This inclusion is enough to conclude that there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Next, we show that there is no proximity bias toward subnetworks with inactive neurons in different situations: when one neuron is inactive in every hidden layer, when a neuron of the first hidden layer is inactive and the subnetwork is small enough, when a neuron of the last hidden layer is inactive and the earlier layers are wide enough, and, for analytic activations or polynomial activations of sufficiently high degree, when a neuron of any hidden layer is inactive.

All hidden layers.

The idea behind Theorem 3.4 can be generalized to deep MLPs when our submodel is defined by having an inactive neuron in every hidden layer, which we call an inactive path (cf. Alexandr and Montúfar (2027)).

Theorem 3.10 (No bias toward inactive paths).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of an MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,d1,…,dL−1,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{L-1},d_{L}) and let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel with architecture (d0,d1−1,…,dL−1−1,dL)(d_{0},d_{1}-1,\dots,d_{L-1}-1,d_{L}). Assume the activations are continuous. Then,

Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′.\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.
Proof idea.

Using the inactive path we construct tangent directions ρL−1∘⋯∘ρ1(⟨w,x⟩+β)v\rho_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ\rho_{1}(\langle w,x\rangle+\beta)\;v for all f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, and these directions span a dense subset of ℋ\mathcal{H}. ∎

Last hidden layer.

We use the observation that a deep MLP is a shallow MLP whose input space is a space of functions rather than the vector space ℝd0\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}. For a parameter θ=(𝐖,𝐛)\theta=(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}) let

hθ=ρL−2∘AL−2∘⋯∘ρ1∘A1:ℝd0→ℝdL−2h_{\theta}=\rho_{L-2}\circ A_{L-2}\circ\dots\circ\rho_{1}\circ A_{1}\colon\ \mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{L-2}}

be the feature map computed by the first L−2L-2 layers (hθ​(x)=xh_{\theta}(x)=x for L=2L=2). Fixing these layers gives a shallow MLP on the features hθh_{\theta}:

fθ​(x)=bL+∑i=1dL−1ρL−1​(⟨wi,hθ​(x)⟩+βi)​vi,f_{\theta}(x)=b_{L}+\sum_{i=1}^{d_{L-1}}\rho_{L-1}\bigl(\langle w_{i},h_{\theta}(x)\rangle+\beta_{i}\bigr)\,v_{i},

where wiw_{i} is the ii-th row of WL−1W_{L-1}, viv_{i} the ii-th column of WLW_{L}, and βi\beta_{i} the ii-th entry of bL−1b_{L-1}. For fixed weights in the first L−2L-2 layers, a neuron in the last hidden layer computes ρL−1∘q\rho_{L-1}\circ q with qq in the space of functions Vθ=span⁡{1,hθ,1,…,hθ,dL−2}V_{\theta}=\operatorname{span}\{1,h_{\theta,1},\dots,h_{\theta,d_{L-2}}\} spanned by the features, just as a neuron of a shallow network computes ρ∘q\rho\circ q with q∈span⁡{1,x1,…,xd0}q\in\operatorname{span}\{1,x_{1},\dots,x_{d_{0}}\}: the deep network is a shallow network whose input space is the function space VθV_{\theta}. In the language of kernel methods, VθV_{\theta} is the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the kernel kθ​(x,x′)=1+⟨hθ​(x),hθ​(x′)⟩k_{\theta}(x,x^{\prime})=1+\langle h_{\theta}(x),h_{\theta}(x^{\prime})\rangle.

This viewpoint explains what happens when neurons in the last hidden layer (L−1)(L-1) are inactive. Define

𝒞θ={ρL−1(⟨w,hθ⟩+β)v:w∈ℝdL−2,β∈ℝ,v∈ℝdL},\mathcal{C}_{\theta}=\!\{\rho_{L-1}(\langle w,h_{\theta}\rangle+\beta)v:w\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{L-2}},\beta\in\mathbb{R},v\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}}\!\},

the set of functions computed by a single neuron of the last hidden layer with input features hθh_{\theta}, which is a symmetric cone. We say that θ\theta has complete features if the span of 𝒞θ\mathcal{C}_{\theta} is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}, that is, the deep network has the same expressivity as a shallow network defined on a function space. For polynomials, this occurs when hidden layers are wide enough (see Corollary 3.12). In the following, a representation of f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is a subnetwork parameter θ\theta with fθ=ff_{\theta}=f.

Proposition 3.11.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of an MLP with arbitrary activations, L≥3L\geq 3 layers, dL−1≥2d_{L-1}\geq 2 and let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the subnetwork with one neuron of the last hidden layer inactive. If every f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime} has a representation with complete features, then Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

The deleted neuron of the last hidden layer can be put back with arbitrary incoming weights ww and arbitrarily small outgoing weights vv of either sign. This gives lines in ℱ\mathcal{F} through ff in the directions ρL−1​(⟨w,hθ⟩+β)​v∈𝒞θ\rho_{L-1}(\langle w,h_{\theta}\rangle+\beta)v\in\mathcal{C}_{\theta}. So Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f) is orthogonal to span⁡𝒞θ\operatorname{span}\mathcal{C}_{\theta}, and it is zero for complete features. ∎

Corollary 3.12.

Under the assumptions of Proposition 3.11 with nonconstant polynomial activations of degree r1,…,rL−1,1r_{1},\dots,r_{L-1},1, if dk≥(d0+r1⋯rkd0)−1d_{k}\geq\binom{d_{0}+r_{1}\cdots r_{k}}{d_{0}}-1 for all k=1,…,L−2k=1,\dots,L-2, then Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

If the first L−2L-2 layers are wide enough, they can compute a basis of all polynomials of degree at most r1⋯rL−2r_{1}\cdots r_{L-2}. Every function of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} can be computed in this basis, and then a single new neuron in layer L−1L-1 gives all polynomials of degree at most r1⋯rL−1r_{1}\cdots r_{L-1}, so the features are complete. ∎

First hidden layer.

The question of what happens when a neuron is deleted in the first layer reduces to the shallow setting of Section 3.1, but with a different loss. Cut the MLP after the affine map of layer 2: f𝐖,𝐛=Ψ∘zf_{\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}}=\Psi\circ z, where z=W2​ρ~​(W1​x+b1)+b2z=W_{2}\tilde{\rho}(W_{1}x+b_{1})+b_{2} is a shallow MLP with architecture (d0,d1,d2)(d_{0},d_{1},d_{2}) and Ψ\Psi is the map computed by the remaining layers. This gives the pulled-back loss ℓ~h​(z)=ℓh​(Ψ∘z)\tilde{\ell}_{h}(z)=\ell_{h}(\Psi\circ z), which may be degenerate. Indeed, its gradient ∇ℓ~h(z)=J⊤∇ℓh(f)\nabla\tilde{\ell}_{h}(z)=J^{\top}\nabla\ell_{h}(f), with J=D​Ψ∘zJ=D\Psi\circ z, vanishes whenever ∇ℓh​(f)∈ker⁡J⊤\nabla\ell_{h}(f)\in\ker J^{\top}. Local Voronoi cells may not be trivial, but we can exclude proximity bias when ℱ′\mathcal{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} is small enough.

Proposition 3.13.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of a deep MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,…,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{L}) and nonconstant polynomial activations 𝛒\bm{\rho}. Let deg⁡ρ1=r1\deg\rho_{1}=r_{1} and let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel with width d1−1d_{1}-1 in the first hidden layer and all other layers unchanged. If

dimℱ′<(d0+r1d0)=dimℝ​[x1,…,xd0]≤r1\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\binom{d_{0}+r_{1}}{d_{0}}=\dim\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d_{0}}]_{\leq r_{1}}

then there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

The reinserted neuron gives more linearly independent directions than the dimension of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, so the union of translated normal cones from Proposition 2.2 has positive codimension. ∎

Any hidden layer.

A neuron of hidden layer kk combines both situations. It reads the features computed by the previous layers, as in the last layer, and its output is processed by the subsequent layers, as in the first layer. Cutting after the affine map of layer k+1k+1, fθ=Ψ∘zf_{\theta}=\Psi\circ z, where zz is a shallow network on the features hθ(k−1)h_{\theta}^{(k-1)} trained with the pulled-back loss ℓ~h​(z)=ℓh​(Ψ∘z)\tilde{\ell}_{h}(z)=\ell_{h}(\Psi\circ z).

For polynomial MLPs, there is no proximity bias toward a submodel ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} with width dk−1d_{k}-1 in a hidden layer kk, provided the djd_{j} are sufficiently high, by Proposition 3.13 and Corollary 3.12. The width conditions are that dj≥(d0+r1⋯rjd0)−1d_{j}\geq\binom{d_{0}+r_{1}\cdots r_{j}}{d_{0}}-1 for all j<kj<k and we also require dimℱ′<(d0+r1⋯rkd0)\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\binom{d_{0}+r_{1}\cdots r_{k}}{d_{0}}.

These width conditions can be dropped when the activation in layer kk has sufficiently high degree.

Proposition 3.14.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of a deep MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,…,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{L}) and nonconstant polynomial activations 𝛒\bm{\rho}, and let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel with width dk−1d_{k}-1 in a hidden layer kk. If deg⁡ρk≥dimℱ′\deg\rho_{k}\geq\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

The functions computed by a single neuron in layer kk span all polynomials of degree at most deg⁡ρk\deg\rho_{k} in the features, which gives deg⁡ρk+1>dimℱ′\deg\rho_{k}+1>\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime} linearly independent constraints on the normal cones. Hence, a dimension count as in Proposition 3.13 concludes the proof. ∎

For non-polynomial activations, no condition on the dimension of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is needed.

Theorem 3.15.

Given a compactly supported finite Borel measure μ≠0\mu\neq 0 on ℝd0\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}} with a Lebesgue density, let ℱ⊆L2​(μ,ℝdL)\mathcal{F}\subseteq L^{2}(\mu,\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}}) be the neural model of an MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,…,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{L}) and analytic nonconstant activations. Let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel given by the subarchitecture with width dk−1d_{k}-1 in a hidden layer kk, and suppose that ρk\rho_{k} is not polynomial. Then, there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Moreover, if k=1k=1 and dL=1d_{L}=1, then Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof idea.

For analytic nonpolynomial ρk\rho_{k}, a single neuron can approximate every function of the features, and JJ vanishes only on a measure zero set. The normal cones need not vanish, but they satisfy more linearly independent constraints than ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} has parameters. Dimension counts on finite-dimensional slices and the Baire category theorem conclude the proof. ∎

It remains to understand what happens when we have an inactive neuron in an arbitrary hidden layer for polynomial neural networks with low activation degrees. In some cases, we may obtain a proper submodel ℱ′⊊ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subsetneq\mathcal{F} with dimℱ′=dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{F} (e.g., Example B.10), in which case there is proximity bias by Proposition 2.4. We conjecture that having a submodel of smaller dimension is sufficient to rule out proximity bias, and provide numerical evidence in Appendix F.

Conjecture 3.16.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of an MLP with polynomial activations, and consider the submodel ℱ′⊂ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{F} obtained by making some hidden neurons inactive. If dimℱ′<dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\dim\mathcal{F}, then there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

4 Lightning Self-Attention

We next study proximity bias in lightning self-attention, following the setup of Henry et al. (2025). Let X∈ℝd×tX\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times t} contain tt input tokens, and let Q,K∈ℝa×dQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times d} and V∈ℝd′×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d} be the query, key, and value matrices. Softmax self-attention takes the form

X⟼V​X​softmax⁡(X⊤​K⊤​Q​X),X\longmapsto VX\operatorname{softmax}\bigl(X^{\top}K^{\top}QX\bigr),

where softmax is applied columnwise. Lightning self-attention omits the softmax normalization, giving

X⟼V​X​X⊤​K⊤​Q​X.X\longmapsto VXX^{\top}K^{\top}QX.

Since KK and QQ enter only through A=K⊤​QA=K^{\top}Q, we reparametrize the model as

ϕ⁡(A,V)​(X)=V​X​X⊤​A​X,rank⁡(A)≤a,\phi(A,V)(X)=VXX^{\top}AX,\qquad\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq a,

and write

𝒳a={ϕ(A,V):rank(A)≤a,V∈ℝd′×d}.\mathcal{X}_{a}=\{\phi(A,V):\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq a,\ V\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d}\}.

Each output coordinate is a homogeneous cubic polynomial in the d​tdt entries of XX. Throughout our analysis of lightning attention, the ambient space is therefore ℋ=ℝd′×t⊗ℝ​[x1,…,xd​t]3,\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times t}\otimes\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\dots,x_{dt}]_{3}, equipped with a fixed inner product.

For s<as<a, let 𝒳s⊆𝒳a\mathcal{X}_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{a} be the submodel consisting of functions in 𝒳a\mathcal{X}_{a} that have a parametrization with rank⁡(A)≤s\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq s. Thus, 𝒳1⊆𝒳2⊆⋯⊆𝒳a.\mathcal{X}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{a}. Our goal is to determine whether there is proximity bias toward these lower-rank submodels or singular loci of the model. The singular locus need not be a submodel obtained by lowering the rank constraint, so we consider singularities separately. The answer depends on the number of tokens and on the rank. For multiple-token attention, there is no proximity bias toward any proper lower-rank submodel. The only multiple-token proximity bias occurs in the case a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1. For single-token attention, the rank constraint creates boundary strata that give proximity bias.

4.1 Multiple-Token Attention

The multiple-token case is t>1t>1. We assume without loss of generality that a≤da\leq d, since for a>da>d the rank constraint is vacuous and 𝒳a−1=𝒳a\mathcal{X}_{a-1}=\mathcal{X}_{a}. For a>1a>1, there is no proximity bias toward any proper lower-rank attention submodel.

Theorem 4.1.

Assume t>1t>1, and 1<a≤d1<a\leq d. Then there is no proximity bias toward 𝒳s\mathcal{X}_{s} for any s<as<a.

Proof idea.

At a function with rank⁡A<a\operatorname{rank}A<a, every rank-one change of AA and every change of VV is a two-sided tangent direction. Outside a small exceptional locus these directions span a space of dimension dim𝒳d\dim\mathcal{X}_{d}, so a dimension count shows that the translated normal cones are small enough. ∎

We next ask whether there is proximity bias toward singular points of the attention model. The algebraic description of the singular loci, obtained by complexifying and projectivizing, is given in Appendix D. For 1<a<d1<a<d, the real singular locus is 𝒳a−1\mathcal{X}_{a-1}. When a=da=d, it is contained in 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}. Thus, Theorem 4.1 implies no proximity bias toward the real singular locus for any a>1a>1.

It remains to consider a=1a=1. There is no nonzero lower-rank submodel in this case, but the singular-locus question can still be posed. When d′>1d^{\prime}>1, the nonzero real singular locus is the rank-one locus

Z={ϕ⁡(A,V):rank⁡(A)=rank⁡(V)=1},Z=\{\phi(A,V):\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(V)=1\},

and again there is no proximity bias toward it.

Proposition 4.2.

Assume that t>1t>1, d>1d>1, a=1a=1, and d′>1d^{\prime}>1. Then there is no proximity bias toward the real singular locus of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}.

Proof idea.

Dimension count for the singular locus ZZ, via unique factorization and birationality. ∎

The scalar-output case d′=1d^{\prime}=1 is different. Writing A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top} and V=v⊤V=v^{\top}, with k,q,v∈ℝdk,q,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, gives

ϕ⁡(A,V)​(X)=(v⊤​X​X⊤​k)​q⊤​X.\phi(A,V)(X)=\bigl(v^{\top}XX^{\top}k\bigr)q^{\top}X.

Since X​X⊤XX^{\top} is symmetric, the parametrization is invariant under exchanging vv and kk, and is therefore generically two-to-one. Setting S=12​(v​k⊤+k​v⊤)S=\tfrac{1}{2}(vk^{\top}+kv^{\top}) removes this symmetry and gives

ϕ⁡(A,V)​(X)=(∑j=1txj⊤​S​xj)​q⊤​X,\phi(A,V)(X)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{t}x_{j}^{\top}Sx_{j}\right)q^{\top}X,

where xjx_{j} is the jj-th column of XX. We therefore write ψ⁡(q,S)​(X)=ϕ⁡(A,V)​(X)\psi(q,S)(X)=\phi(A,V)(X) and define

U={ψ(q,S):q∈ℝd,rank(S)≤1}.U=\{\psi(q,S):q\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 1\}.

In terms of the original parameters, rank⁡(S)≤1\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 1 exactly when vv and kk are linearly dependent.

Theorem 4.3.

Assume t>1t>1, a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1, and d>1d>1. There is proximity bias toward UU. If d>2d>2, UU is both the real singular locus of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} and a boundary of the real model. If d=2d=2, UU is a boundary of the real model.

Proof idea.

A real inertia constraint makes UU one-sided, and the Voronoi cell of UU fills an open set. ∎

The two geometric regimes in Theorem 4.3 are visible already in the smallest dimensions; see Figure 4. By Lemma D.9, the map q⊗S↦ψ⁡(q,S)q\otimes S\mapsto\psi(q,S) is injective for t>1t>1, so these low-dimensional slices faithfully represent the corresponding geometry of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}. For d=2d=2, the locus UU appears as a boundary of the real model despite the algebraic model being smooth, whereas for d=3d=3 it appears as a singular locus.

The multiple-token case is summarized as follows.

Regime a>1a>1 or d′>1d^{\prime}>1 a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1
proximity bias? No Yes

4.2 Single-Token Attention

The geometry of the attention model changes when t=1t=1. Writing S=12​(A+A⊤)S=\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{\top}), we reparametrize using a symmetric matrix S∈S2​(ℝd)S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and V∈ℝd′×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d}:

ψ⁡(S,V)​(x)=(V​x)​(x⊤​S​x).\psi(S,V)(x)=(Vx)(x^{\top}Sx).

For t>1t>1, the fiber is controlled by the bilinear form y⊤​A​xy^{\top}Ax, where rank one is the exceptional reducible case. For t=1t=1, this is replaced by the quadratic form x⊤​S​xx^{\top}Sx, which is reducible over ℂ\mathbb{C} when rank⁡(S)≤2\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2. Consequently, rank-two symmetric matrices now appear in the singular locus.

The rank constraint is also different under symmetrization. Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, matrices AA with rank⁡(A)≤a\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq a give the symmetric matrices SS with rank⁡(S)≤min⁡{2​a,d}\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq\min\{2a,d\}, whereas over ℝ\mathbb{R} they give those SS with at most aa positive and at most aa negative eigenvalues. These two observations lead to the following.

Theorem 4.4.

Assume that t=1t=1.

  1. 1.

    If a=d>1a=d>1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1, then

    Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳dℂ))=ℙ⁡({ψ⁡(S,V):rank⁡(V)=1,rank⁡(S)≤2}),\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{d}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}\left(\left\{\psi(S,V):\begin{matrix}\operatorname{rank}(V)=1,\\ \operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2\end{matrix}\right\}\right),

    and there is no proximity bias toward the corresponding real singular locus.

  2. 2.

    If a>1a>1 and 2​a<d2a<d, then

    Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ))=ℙ⁡({ψ⁡(S,V):rank⁡(S)≤2​a−1}).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\psi(S,V):\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2a-1\}\bigr).

    The real model 𝒳a\mathcal{X}_{a} exhibits proximity bias toward the rank-(2​a−1)(2a-1) stratum UU where SS has inertia (a,a−1,d−2​a+1)(a,a-1,d-2a+1).

Proof idea.

Part 1 is a dimension count as in Proposition 4.2. Part 2 is a one-sided argument that implies full-dimensional Voronoi cells, as in Theorem 4.3. ∎

Thus, the larger singular locus in the single-token setting does not by itself produce proximity bias. In the first regime, the rank-two factorization locus is singular but there is no proximity bias toward it. In the second, proximity bias arises from the one-sided boundary induced by the real inertia constraint, paralleling the boundary mechanism in Theorem 4.3. Proofs are given in Appendix E.

4.3 Beyond lightning self-attention

Theorem 4.3 identifies a proximity bias toward UU in rank-one scalar-output lightning attention. We ask whether this proximity bias is visible under gradient-based training after replacing lightning attention by softmax attention. The change in identifiability caused by normalization is studied in Henry et al. (2025); here we compare the training dynamics empirically.

We take d=t=2d=t=2 and a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1. In each run, the target is h=ψ⁡(q∗,S∗)h=\psi(q_{\ast},S_{\ast}), where q∗∈ℝ2q_{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} is a unit vector and S∗≻0S_{\ast}\succ 0 has eigenvalues 11 and 0.20.2. We sample 512512 standard Gaussian inputs XiX_{i} and use the labels h⁡(Xi)h(X_{i}) for both models. We initialize from k0,q∗,v0k_{0},q_{\ast},v_{0}, with S0=12​(v0​k0⊤+k0​v0⊤)S_{0}=\frac{1}{2}(v_{0}k_{0}^{\top}+k_{0}v_{0}^{\top}) having eigenvalues 11 and −0.05-0.05, and train k,q,vk,q,v for 500500 steps using Adam and squared loss. For softmax attention, the only change is replacing ϕ⁡(A,V)​(X)=V​X​X⊤​A​X\phi(A,V)(X)=VXX^{\top}AX by V​X​softmax⁡(X⊤​A​X).VX\operatorname{softmax}(X^{\top}AX).

At training step tt, let St=12​(vt​kt⊤+kt​vt⊤).S_{t}=\frac{1}{2}(v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}+k_{t}v_{t}^{\top}). Figure 5 shows σ2​(St)/σ1​(St)\sigma_{2}(S_{t})/\sigma_{1}(S_{t}). For lightning attention, the ratio rapidly converges to zero, consistent with Theorem 4.3. For softmax, the ratio decreases at a slower rate.

5 Discussion

Our results show that preference for submodels is not caused by singularities alone. In the models studied here, most lower-rank or inactive-neuron submodels are not preferred, even when they lie in the singular locus of the neural model. The exceptional cases reflect the real geometry, such as one-sided boundary strata or large normal cones. In lightning self-attention, proximity bias arises at one-sided boundaries coming from a real inertia constraint.

It is natural to generalize these results to more expressive models. Low-rank matrix approximation is the starting point, from which one can move toward neural models along two natural hierarchies:

matrix rank\displaystyle\text{matrix rank} ⟶tensor rank\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{tensor rank}
⟶shallow MLPs\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{shallow MLPs}
⟶deep MLPs⟶⋯,\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{deep MLPs}\longrightarrow\cdots,
matrix rank\displaystyle\text{matrix rank} ⟶lightning self-attention\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{lightning self-attention}
⟶self-attention⟶⋯.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{self-attention}\longrightarrow\cdots.

This paper takes steps along both hierarchies: from tensor rank and shallow MLPs toward deep networks, and from low-rank matrix approximation to lightning self-attention. The next steps are to understand preference for submodels in deep polynomial MLPs with arbitrary activation degrees when a neuron from any hidden layer is inactive (cf. Conjecture 3.16) and softmax self-attention. More broadly, when the geometry itself does not prefer a simpler submodel, an important question is whether preferences observed in practice come from the optimization dynamics or from structure in the target.

See 2.2

Lemma A.1.

Let ℓ:ℋ→ℝ\ell:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R} be Fréchet differentiable. If f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} is a local minimizer of ℓ|ℱ\ell\rvert_{\mathcal{F}} then −∇ℓ​(f)∈Nℱ​(f)-\nabla\ell(f)\in N_{\mathcal{F}}(f).

Proof.

Let v∈Tℱ​(f)v\in T_{\mathcal{F}}(f) and pick sequences (fn)n⊂ℱ(f_{n})_{n}\subset\mathcal{F} and (τn)n⊂ℝ>0(\tau_{n})_{n}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0} such that (fn−f)/τn→v(f_{n}-f)/\tau_{n}\to v. Since ff is a local minimizer, ℓ⁡(fn)−ℓ⁡(f)≥0\ell(f_{n})-\ell(f)\geq 0 for all sufficiently large nn. By Fréchet differentiability of ℓ\ell,

ℓ⁡(fn)−ℓ⁡(f)=⟨∇ℓ​(f),fn−f⟩+o⁡(‖fn−f‖).\ell(f_{n})-\ell(f)=\langle\nabla\ell(f),f_{n}-f\rangle+o(\|f_{n}-f\|).

Dividing by τn\tau_{n} and taking the limit gives ⟨∇ℓ​(f),v⟩≥0\langle\nabla\ell(f),v\rangle\geq 0. ∎

Proof of Proposition 2.2.

We always have f∈Vorℱ⁡(f)f\in\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(f) because ℓf​(f)=0\ell_{f}(f)=0 and ℓf≥0\ell_{f}\geq 0. If h∈Vorℱ⁡(f)h\in\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(f), then ff is a global, and hence local, minimizer of ℓh\ell_{h}. If ff is a local minimizer, Lemma A.1 gives −∇ℓh​(f)=2​(h−f)∈Nℱ​(f)-\nabla\ell_{h}(f)=2(h-f)\in N_{\mathcal{F}}(f). Since Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f) is a cone, h∈f+Nℱ​(f)h\in f+N_{\mathcal{F}}(f). ∎

Corollary A.2.

If Nℱ​(f)={0}N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)=\{0\} for every f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, then Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

Proof of Proposition 2.4.

Then, ℱ¯\overline{\mathcal{F}} has a point f~\tilde{f} closest to hh, and ‖h−f~‖≤‖h−f‖≤ε\|h-\tilde{f}\|\leq\|h-f\|\leq\varepsilon, so ‖f~−f‖≤2​ε\|\tilde{f}-f\|\leq 2\varepsilon and f~∈ℱ′\tilde{f}\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Appendix B Proofs of Multilayer Perceptron Results

B.1 Shallow MLPs

See 3.4

A cone in a real Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} is a set 𝒞⊆ℋ\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{H} that is closed under multiplication by nonnegative scalars, that is, f∈𝒞,λ≥0⟹λ​f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C},\lambda\geq 0\implies\lambda f\in\mathcal{C}. A cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} is symmetric if 𝒞=−𝒞\mathcal{C}=-\mathcal{C}. Equivalently, a symmetric cone is a set 𝒞⊆ℋ\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{H} that is closed under multiplication by scalars: f∈𝒞,λ∈ℝ⟹λ​f∈𝒞.f\in\mathcal{C},\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\implies\lambda f\in\mathcal{C}.

Lemma B.1.

If 𝒞⊆ℋ\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{H} is a symmetric cone whose linear span is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}, then its polar cone is zero.

Proof.

The polar cone of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is equal to its orthogonal complement, because 𝒞\mathcal{C} is symmetric. The orthogonal complement of 𝒞\mathcal{C} equals the orthogonal complement of its linear span, so it is zero. ∎

Lemma B.2.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a symmetric cone whose linear span is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}. If ℱ′+𝒞⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{F}, then Nℱ​(f)={0}N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)=\{0\} for all f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, and Nℱ¯​(f)={0}N_{\overline{\mathcal{F}}}(f)=\{0\} for all f∈ℱ′¯f\in\overline{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. Therefore,

Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)=ℱ′andVorℱ¯⁡(ℱ′¯)=Vorℱ¯loc⁡(ℱ′¯)=ℱ′¯.\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{Vor}_{\overline{\mathcal{F}}}\left(\overline{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\right)=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\overline{\mathcal{F}}}\left(\overline{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\right)=\overline{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}.
Proof.

It suffices to show that Tℱ​(f)T_{\mathcal{F}}(f) contains 𝒞\mathcal{C} for all f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, by Lemma B.1. Given any v∈𝒞v\in\mathcal{C}, we have fn=f+1n​v∈ℱf_{n}=f+\frac{1}{n}v\in\mathcal{F} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, so v=limn→∞(fn−f)/1n∈Tℱ​(f)v=\lim_{n\to\infty}(f_{n}-f)/\frac{1}{n}\in T_{\mathcal{F}}(f). Similarly, if f∈ℱ′¯f\in\overline{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} and v∈𝒞v\in\mathcal{C}, then fn=f+1n​v∈ℱ¯f_{n}=f+\frac{1}{n}v\in\overline{\mathcal{F}}, so the same argument applies. The claims about (local) Voronoi cells follow from Proposition 2.2. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Consider the single-neuron cone

𝒞={f(x)=ρ(⟨w1,x⟩+β)w2+b:w1∈ℝd0,β∈ℝ,w2,b∈ℝd2}.\mathcal{C}=\left\{f(x)=\rho(\langle w_{1},x\rangle+\beta)w_{2}+b:w_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}},\beta\in\mathbb{R},w_{2},b\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}\right\}.

Then ℱ′=∑i=1d1−1𝒞\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{1}-1}\mathcal{C} and ℱ=ℱ′+𝒞\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\mathcal{C}. The linear span of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}, because span⁡(𝒞)=span⁡(ℱ)\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{C})=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{F}). Therefore, the statement follows from Lemma B.2 and Corollary A.2. ∎

B.2 Deep MLPs

Neural models of shallow MLPs are sums of cones. This no longer holds for deep MLPs. However, in some cases, we can still find a cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} whose span is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H} and such that ℱ′+𝒞⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{F}. In such cases, Lemma B.2 implies that ℱ′=Vorℱ⁡(ℱ′)=Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}). Note that unlike in the shallow case we may not have the equality ℱ′+𝒞=ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{F}.

We define the features of layer jj recursively by hθ(0)​(x)=xh^{(0)}_{\theta}(x)=x and hθ(j)=ρj​(Wj​hθ(j−1)+bj)h^{(j)}_{\theta}=\rho_{j}(W_{j}h^{(j-1)}_{\theta}+b_{j}); then fθ=WL​hθ(L−1)+bLf_{\theta}=W_{L}h^{(L-1)}_{\theta}+b_{L}, and we write hθ=hθ(L−2)h_{\theta}=h^{(L-2)}_{\theta} for the features that feed the last hidden layer, as in Section 3.2. We consider two scenarios, as in Section 3: (1) all activations are polynomials and ℋ=span⁡ℱ\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{span}\mathcal{F} is finite-dimensional with any inner product, (2) the activations are continuous, μ\mu is a finite Borel measure with compact support KK, and ℋ=span⁡ℱ¯⊆L2​(μ,ℝdL)\mathcal{H}=\overline{\operatorname{span}\mathcal{F}}\subseteq L^{2}(\mu;\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}}). The loss that we use is the squared distance ℓh​(f)=‖h−f‖2\ell_{h}(f)=\|h-f\|^{2}. We write 𝒫≤n=ℝ​[x1,…,xd0]≤n\mathcal{P}_{\leq n}=\mathbb{R}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d_{0}}]_{\leq n} for the polynomials of degree at most nn in d0d_{0} variables, so dim𝒫≤n=(d0+nd0)\dim\mathcal{P}_{\leq n}=\binom{d_{0}+n}{d_{0}}.

See 3.10

Lemma B.3.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of an MLP with architecture 𝐝=(d0,d1,…,dL−1,dL)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{L-1},d_{L}), let ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} be the submodel with architecture (d0,d1−1,…,dL−1−1,dL)(d_{0},d_{1}-1,\dots,d_{L-1}-1,d_{L}), and let 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} be the submodel with architecture (d0,1,…,1,dL)(d_{0},1,\dots,1,d_{L}). Then 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} is a symmetric cone and ℱ′+𝒞~⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{F}.

Proof.

Given parameters θ′\theta^{\prime} of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and θ~\tilde{\theta} of 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}}, define a parameter θ\theta of ℱ\mathcal{F} with block-diagonal weight matrices Wj=diag⁡(Wj′,W~j)W_{j}=\operatorname{diag}(W^{\prime}_{j},\tilde{W}_{j}) and biases bj=(bj′,b~j)b_{j}=(b^{\prime}_{j},\tilde{b}_{j}), except that W1⊤=(W1′⊤​W~1⊤)W_{1}^{\top}=({W^{\prime}_{1}}^{\top}\ {\tilde{W}_{1}}^{\top}), WL=(WL′​W~L)W_{L}=(W^{\prime}_{L}\ \tilde{W}_{L}) and bL=bL′+b~Lb_{L}=b^{\prime}_{L}+\tilde{b}_{L}. Since activations act coordinatewise, fθ=fθ′+fθ~f_{\theta}=f_{\theta^{\prime}}+f_{\tilde{\theta}}. Scaling (W~L,b~L)(\tilde{W}_{L},\tilde{b}_{L}) scales fθ~f_{\tilde{\theta}}, so 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} is a symmetric cone. ∎

To prove Theorem 3.10 it suffices to show that the span of the symmetric cone 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} of the architecture (d0,1,…,1,dL)(d_{0},1,\dots,1,d_{L}) is dense in ℋ\mathcal{H}, by Lemma B.3 and Lemma B.2. We do this separately for the two cases: the polynomial (finite-dimensional) case, and the case where not all activations are polynomial (which lives in an infinite dimensional function space).

Lemma B.4.

If σ\sigma is a polynomial of degree R≥1R\geq 1, then span⁡{σ⁡(q):q∈𝒫≤n}=𝒫≤R​n\operatorname{span}\{\sigma(q):q\in\mathcal{P}_{\leq n}\}=\mathcal{P}_{\leq Rn}.

Proof.

Let V=span⁡{σ⁡(q):q∈𝒫≤n}V=\operatorname{span}\{\sigma(q):q\in\mathcal{P}_{\leq n}\}. Every polynomial in VV has degree at most R​nRn, hence V⊆𝒫≤R​nV\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\leq Rn}. Conversely, every monomial of degree at most R​nRn is a product m1⋯mkm_{1}\cdots m_{k} of k≤Rk\leq R monomials of degree at most nn. For t∈ℝkt\in\mathbb{R}^{k} and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, the polynomial q=t1​m1+⋯+tk​mk+sq=t_{1}m_{1}+\dots+t_{k}m_{k}+s lies in 𝒫≤n\mathcal{P}_{\leq n}, so σ⁡(q)∈V\sigma(q)\in V. Expanding σ⁡(q)\sigma(q) as a polynomial in (t,s)(t,s), only the top-degree term σR​qR\sigma_{R}q^{R} of σ\sigma contributes to the monomial t1⋯tksR−kt_{1}\cdots t_{k}\,s^{R-k}, and its coefficient is σRR!(R−k)!m1⋯mk\sigma_{R}\frac{R!}{(R-k)!}\,m_{1}\cdots m_{k} with σR≠0\sigma_{R}\neq 0. Since every coefficient of a polynomial map (t,s)↦σ⁡(q)(t,s)\mapsto\sigma(q) with values in VV is a linear combination of finitely many of its values, it lies in VV. Hence m1⋯mk∈Vm_{1}\cdots m_{k}\in V. ∎

In what follows, we use the universal approximation theorem (Leshno et al., 1993), and abbreviate it to UAT: if σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is continuous and not a polynomial, then for every compact set Y⊂ℝmY\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} the functions y↦σ⁡(⟨a,y⟩+b)y\mapsto\sigma(\langle a,y\rangle+b) with a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} span a dense subset of the continuous functions C⁡(Y)C(Y). In our case, since μ\mu is finite with compact support KK, C⁡(K)C(K) is dense in L2​(K)L^{2}(K) and uniform convergence on KK implies convergence in L2​(K)L^{2}(K). The next lemma extends UAT to paths of single neurons, one per hidden layer.

Lemma B.5.

Let activation functions ρ1,…,ρL−1:ℝ→ℝ\rho_{1},\dots,\rho_{L-1}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be continuous and nonconstant, not all polynomials, and let K⊆ℝd0K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}} be compact. Let Πi\Pi_{i} be the set of functions computed by the neuron in layer ii of a network with architecture (d0,1,…,1)(d_{0},1,\dots,1), that is, Π1={ρ1​(⟨a,x⟩+b)}\Pi_{1}=\{\rho_{1}(\langle a,x\rangle+b)\} and Πi={ρi(wp+c):p∈Πi−1,w,c∈ℝ}\Pi_{i}=\{\rho_{i}(wp+c):p\in\Pi_{i-1},\,w,c\in\mathbb{R}\} for 1<i<L1<i<L. Then span⁡ΠL−1\operatorname{span}\Pi_{L-1} is dense in C⁡(K)C(K).

Proof.

Let ViV_{i} be the uniform closure of span⁡Πi\operatorname{span}\Pi_{i} in C⁡(K)C(K). If p∈Πi−1p\in\Pi_{i-1} and φ\varphi is a uniform limit on compact intervals of linear combinations of s↦ρi​(w​s+c)s\mapsto\rho_{i}(ws+c), then φ∘p∈Vi\varphi\circ p\in V_{i}, by substituting s=p⁡(x)s=p(x). The identity φ⁡(s)=s\varphi(s)=s is such a limit: if ρi\rho_{i} is a polynomial of degree R≥1R\geq 1, the functions ρi​(w​s+c)\rho_{i}(ws+c) span all polynomials of degree at most RR in ss by Lemma B.4; otherwise apply UAT with m=1m=1. Hence V1⊆⋯⊆VL−1V_{1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq V_{L-1}. Now let ρi\rho_{i} be non-polynomial. Choose wj,cjw_{j},c_{j} so that τ=ρi−1(wi−1ρi−2(⋯ρ1(⋅)⋯)+ci−1)\tau=\rho_{i-1}(w_{i-1}\rho_{i-2}(\cdots\rho_{1}(\cdot)\cdots)+c_{i-1}) is nonconstant (τ=id\tau=\mathrm{id} if i=1i=1). By UAT with input dimension m=1m=1, φ=arctan\varphi=\arctan is a uniform limit on compact intervals of combinations of ρi​(w​s+c)\rho_{i}(ws+c), so ψ⁡(⟨a,x⟩+b)∈Vi\psi(\langle a,x\rangle+b)\in V_{i} for all a,ba,b, where ψ=arctan∘τ\psi=\arctan\circ\tau. Since ψ\psi is bounded and nonconstant, it is not a polynomial, and UAT gives Vi=C⁡(K)V_{i}=C(K). Therefore VL−1=Vi=C⁡(K)V_{L-1}=V_{i}=C(K). ∎

Next, we show that if the normal cone at each point of a semialgebraic set SS is cut down by at least mm independent linear constraints, then the union of translated normal cones over SS has codimension at least m−dimSm-\dim S. When m>dimSm>\dim S, this union has positive codimension, ruling out proximity bias toward SS by Proposition 2.2.

Lemma B.8.

Let Θ⊆ℝP\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{P} be semialgebraic and let Φ,v1,…,vr:Θ→ℋ\Phi,v_{1},\dots,v_{r}\colon\Theta\to\mathcal{H} be semialgebraic maps with Φ⁡(Θ)⊆ℱ\Phi(\Theta)\subseteq\mathcal{F} and Nℱ​(Φ⁡(θ))⟂vi​(θ)N_{\mathcal{F}}(\Phi(\theta))\perp v_{i}(\theta) for all θ,i\theta,i. Let n=dimℋn=\dim\mathcal{H}, let S⊆Φ⁡(Θ)S\subseteq\Phi(\Theta) be semialgebraic and assume that for every f∈Sf\in S the vectors vi​(θ)v_{i}(\theta) with Φ⁡(θ)=f\Phi(\theta)=f span a space of dimension at least mm. Then ⋃f∈S(f+Nℱ​(f))\bigcup_{f\in S}(f+N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)) lies in a semialgebraic set of dimension at most dimS+n−m\dim S+n-m.

Proof.

The set E={(f,ν)∈S×ℋ:∀θ⁡(Φ⁡(θ)=f⇒⟨ν,vi​(θ)⟩=0​∀i)}E=\{(f,\nu)\in S\times\mathcal{H}:\ \forall\theta\,(\Phi(\theta)=f\Rightarrow\langle\nu,v_{i}(\theta)\rangle=0\ \forall i)\} is semialgebraic, by the Tarski–Seidenberg Theorem. Its fiber over ff is a linear space of dimension at most n−mn-m containing Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f), so dimE≤dimS+n−m\dim E\leq\dim S+n-m, and {f+ν:(f,ν)∈E}\{f+\nu:(f,\nu)\in E\} is its image under a linear map. ∎

The following example shows that the bound in Proposition B.9 is sharp.

Example B.10 (Rank two versus rank three).

Let 𝐝=(2,3,1,1)\mathbf{d}=(2,3,1,1) and ρ1=ρ2:t↦t3\rho_{1}=\rho_{2}:t\mapsto t^{3}, and no bias terms. Every real binary cubic is a sum of three cubes of real linear forms, and it is a sum of two cubes if and only if it is a cube or has negative discriminant (one real and two complex conjugate roots); see, e.g., Comon and Ottaviani (2012). Hence ℱ={p3:p​ a binary cubic}\mathcal{F}=\{p^{3}:p\text{ a binary cubic}\} and ℱ′={p3:disc⁡(p)<0}∪{ℓ9}\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\{p^{3}:\operatorname{disc}(p)<0\}\cup\{\ell^{9}\}: the model consists of the cubes of the cubics of real rank at most three, the submodel of those of real rank at most two. Since p↦p3p\mapsto p^{3} is injective, dimℱ′=dimℱ=4\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{F}=4, and ℱ′≠ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\neq\mathcal{F}. By Proposition 2.4 the local Voronoi cell Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) has nonempty interior: every target close to p03p_{0}^{3} with disc⁡(p0)<0\operatorname{disc}(p_{0})<0 has all its nearest points of ℱ\mathcal{F} in ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Here dimℱ′=4=(2+3−13)\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=4=\binom{2+3-1}{3}, so the bound in Proposition B.9 cannot be relaxed.

Lemma B.11.

For every continuous γ:ℝdk−1→ℝ\gamma\colon\mathbb{R}^{d_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R} and every ll: J​el​(γ∘η)∈ℋJe_{l}\,(\gamma\circ\eta)\in\mathcal{H} and Nℱ​(fθ′)⟂J​el​(γ∘η)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f_{\theta^{\prime}})\perp Je_{l}\,(\gamma\circ\eta).

Lemma B.12.

Let μ\mu have a Lebesgue density. (i) A real-analytic function on ℝd0\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}} that is not identically zero vanishes only on a set of Lebesgue measure zero. (ii) If fθ′f_{\theta^{\prime}} is not constant, there are ll and a nonconstant coordinate ηi\eta_{i} of η\eta such that J​el≠0Je_{l}\neq 0 μ\mu-almost everywhere, and for every NN the functions J​el​ηijJe_{l}\,\eta_{i}^{\,j}, 0≤j≤N0\leq j\leq N, are linearly independent in ℋ\mathcal{H}.

(ii) D​fθ′=J​D​z≠0Df_{\theta^{\prime}}=J\,Dz\neq 0, so some entry of some column J​elJe_{l} is a nonzero analytic function, nonzero almost everywhere by (i). Since fθ′f_{\theta^{\prime}} is a function of η\eta, some ηi\eta_{i} is nonconstant. If J​el​p​(ηi)=0Je_{l}\,p(\eta_{i})=0 almost everywhere for a polynomial pp, then p⁡(ηi)=0p(\eta_{i})=0 almost everywhere. Therefore, (i) implies that p=0p=0 on the interval ηi​(ℝd0)\eta_{i}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}), so p=0p=0. ∎

Lemma B.13.

Let VV be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, Θ⊆ℝP\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{P} compact, and A:Θ→Hom⁡(V,ℝM)A\colon\Theta\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,\mathbb{R}^{M}), c:Θ→ℝMc\colon\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^{M} Lipschitz with rank⁡A⁡(θ)≥P+1\operatorname{rank}A(\theta)\geq P+1 for all θ\theta. Appendix C Convolutional neural networks

A one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with L≥2L\geq 2 layers, filters wl∈ℝklw_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{l}} and strides sls_{l} is the map

f𝐰(x)=wL⋆sLσ(⋯σ(w1⋆s1x)),f_{\mathbf{w}}(x)=w_{L}\star_{s_{L}}\sigma\bigl(\cdots\,\sigma(w_{1}\star_{s_{1}}x)\bigr),

where (w⋆sh)​[i]=∑j=1kw⁡[j]​h​[s⁡(i−1)+j](w\star_{s}h)[i]=\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}w[j]\,h[s(i-1)+j], with one channel and no bias terms. We assume that the activation σ\sigma is a generic polynomial of large enough degree depending on LL (Shahverdi et al., 2026) such that σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0. Then the neural model ℱ={f𝐰}\mathcal{F}=\{f_{\mathbf{w}}\} is a semialgebraic subset of a finite-dimensional space ℋ\mathcal{H} of polynomial maps, which we equip with any inner product. The natural submodels have smaller filters: for integers 0≤Al<kl0\leq A_{l}<k_{l}, not all zero, ℱ𝐀\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{A}} consists of the functions f𝐰f_{\mathbf{w}} such that, for every ll, the first or the last AlA_{l} entries of wlw_{l} vanish.

Proposition C.1.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the neural model of a CNN with a generic polynomial activation σ\sigma of large enough degree such that σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, and let ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F} be a semialgebraic subset with dimℱ′<dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\dim\mathcal{F}. Then, Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) is contained in a semialgebraic set of dimension at most dimℋ−(dimℱ−dimℱ′)\dim\mathcal{H}-(\dim\mathcal{F}-\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}). Therefore, ℱ\mathcal{F} exhibits no proximity bias toward any submodel ℱ𝐀\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{A}} with smaller filters, nor toward its singular locus.

Proof.

Let φ:ℝm→ℋ\varphi\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathcal{H}, 𝐰↦f𝐰\mathbf{w}\mapsto f_{\mathbf{w}}, be the parametrization and n=dimℋn=\dim\mathcal{H}. By Shahverdi et al. (2026, Theorem 4.4), d​φ𝐰d\varphi_{\mathbf{w}} is injective whenever f𝐰≠0f_{\mathbf{w}}\neq 0, so dimℱ=m\dim\mathcal{F}=m. We have Nℱ​(f𝐰)⊆(im⁡d​φ𝐰)⟂N_{\mathcal{F}}(f_{\mathbf{w}})\subseteq(\operatorname{im}d\varphi_{\mathbf{w}})^{\perp}, a space of dimension n−mn-m, for every f𝐰∈ℱ′∖{0}f_{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\setminus\{0\}. Hence, ⋃f∈ℱ′∖{0}(f+Nℱ​(f))\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\setminus\{0\}}(f+N_{\mathcal{F}}(f)) lies in a semialgebraic set of dimension at most dimℱ′+n−m\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}+n-m, by Lemma B.8. At the origin, t​ℱ⊆ℱt\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{F} for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, so Nℱ​(0)⊆(span⁡ℱ)⟂N_{\mathcal{F}}(0)\subseteq(\operatorname{span}\mathcal{F})^{\perp}, of dimension at most n−mn-m. By Proposition 2.2, Vorℱloc⁡(ℱ′)\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}) lies in a semialgebraic set of dimension at most n−(dimℱ−dimℱ′)<nn-(\dim\mathcal{F}-\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime})<n. Finally, ℱ𝐀\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{A}} is a finite union of images of coordinate subspaces of dimension m−∑lAl<mm-\sum_{l}A_{l}<m, and the singular locus of the Zariski closure XX of ℱ\mathcal{F} is a proper algebraic subset of the irreducible variety XX, so both have dimension less than dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}. The dimension of the normal cone determines whether a lower-dimensional stratum can exhibit proximity bias.
