For the algebraic analysis in this subsection, we work over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let Daℂ={A∈ℂd×d:rank⁡(A)≤a},D_{a}^{\mathbb{C}}=\{A\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}:\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq a\}, let 𝒳aℂ\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}} denote the complexification of 𝒳a\mathcal{X}_{a}, and let ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}}) denote its projectivization. We also set

Zℂ={ϕ(A,V):A∈ℂd×d,V∈ℂd′×d,rank(A)=rank(V)=1}.Z^{\mathbb{C}}=\{\phi(A,V):A\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d},\ V\in\mathbb{C}^{d^{\prime}\times d},\ \operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(V)=1\}.
Lemma D.6.

Assume that either a>1a>1 or d′>1d^{\prime}>1. Then

Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ))={ℙ⁡(𝒳a−1ℂ),1<a<d,ℙ⁡(Zℂ),a=d​ or ​(a=1,d′>1).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\begin{cases}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}),&1<a<d,\\ \mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}),&a=d\text{ or }(a=1,\ d^{\prime}>1).\end{cases}

We first establish the finite-birational statement used in the proof.

Proposition D.7.

The projectivized parametrization ϕ¯:ℙ⁡(Daℂ)×ℙ⁡(ℂd′×d)⟶ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ)\overline{\phi}:\mathbb{P}(D_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})\times\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{\prime}\times d})\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}}) has finite fibers. It is birational when a>1a>1, and also when a=1a=1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1. When a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1, it is generically two-to-one.

Proof.

Suppose that ϕ⁡(A,V)=ϕ⁡(A′,V′)\phi(A,V)=\phi(A^{\prime},V^{\prime}). Since t>1t>1, comparing terms involving two distinct input columns gives (vi⊤y)(y⊤Ax)=(vi′y⊤)(y⊤A′x)(v_{i}^{\top}y)(y^{\top}Ax)=(v_{i}^{\prime}{}^{\top}y)(y^{\top}A^{\prime}x) for every row ii and all x,y∈ℂdx,y\in\mathbb{C}^{d}. If rank⁡(A)>1\operatorname{rank}(A)>1, the bilinear form y⊤​A​xy^{\top}Ax is irreducible. Unique factorization therefore gives A′=λ​AA^{\prime}=\lambda A and V′=λ−1​VV^{\prime}=\lambda^{-1}V, so the projective fiber is a singleton.

Suppose now that rank⁡(A)=1\operatorname{rank}(A)=1 and write A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top}. Unique factorization first gives A′=k′​q⊤A^{\prime}=k^{\prime}q^{\top}, up to scaling, and then (vi⊤y)(k⊤y)=(vi′y⊤)(k′y⊤).(v_{i}^{\top}y)(k^{\top}y)=(v_{i}^{\prime}{}^{\top}y)(k^{\prime}{}^{\top}y). If rank⁡(V)>1\operatorname{rank}(V)>1, two nonproportional rows of VV determine the common factor k⊤​yk^{\top}y, so the projective fiber is again a singleton.

Finally, if rank⁡(V)=1\operatorname{rank}(V)=1, write V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}. Up to scaling, the only possibilities are (A′,V′)=(k​q⊤,h​v⊤)(A^{\prime},V^{\prime})=(kq^{\top},hv^{\top}) or (A′,V′)=(v​q⊤,h​k⊤).(A^{\prime},V^{\prime})=(vq^{\top},hk^{\top}). Thus every projective fiber contains at most two points. Since the source is projective, the map is proper; finite fibers therefore imply that it is finite.

If a>1a>1, a general A∈DaℂA\in D_{a}^{\mathbb{C}} has rank greater than one, so the general fiber is a singleton. If a=1a=1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1, a general VV has rank greater than one, so again the general fiber is a singleton. Hence the map is birational in these cases. If a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1, then for general nonproportional kk and vv the two projective preimages above are distinct, so the map is generically two-to-one. ∎

We also recall the following standard criterion. It is stated in this form in (Kohn et al., 2017, Lemma 3.2); see also (Harris, 1992, Theorem 14.9) for the classical criterion for finite morphisms underlying the result.

Lemma D.8.

Let f:X→Yf:X\to Y be a finite birational surjective morphism between irreducible projective varieties. Then YY is smooth at yy if and only if f−1​(y)f^{-1}(y) consists of a single point xx, the variety XX is smooth at xx, and dx​fd_{x}f is injective.

Proof of Lemma D.6.

Suppose first that 1<a<d1<a<d. If p∈ℙ⁡(𝒳a−1ℂ)p\in\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}), then pp has a preimage with rank⁡(A)<a\operatorname{rank}(A)<a. Since Sing⁡(Daℂ)=Da−1ℂ,\operatorname{Sing}(D_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})=D_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}, the source is singular at this preimage. Hence pp is singular by Lemma D.8.

Conversely, let p∉ℙ⁡(𝒳a−1ℂ)p\notin\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}). Its unique projective preimage has rank⁡(A)=a>1\operatorname{rank}(A)=a>1 by Proposition D.7, and the source is smooth there. The proof of Lemma D.3 is algebraic and applies over ℂ\mathbb{C}; since rank⁡(A)>1\operatorname{rank}(A)>1, its affine kernel consists only of the scaling direction. Thus the projective differential is injective, and pp is smooth by Lemma D.8. Therefore Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ))=ℙ⁡(𝒳a−1ℂ).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}).

Now suppose that a=da=d. The parameter space DdℂD_{d}^{\mathbb{C}} is smooth. Let p∈ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\in\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}), with A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top} and V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}. If kk and vv are not proportional, Proposition D.7 gives two distinct projective preimages. If kk and vv are proportional, the fiber is a singleton, but Lemma D.3 gives a dd-dimensional affine kernel, so the projective differential is not injective. Thus pp is singular in either case.

If p∉ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\notin\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}), its projective fiber is a singleton and the exceptional case in Lemma D.3 does not occur. The source is smooth and the projective differential is injective, so pp is smooth. Therefore Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳dℂ))=ℙ⁡(Zℂ).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{d}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}).

Finally, suppose that a=1a=1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1. The projective determinantal variety ℙ⁡(D1ℂ)\mathbb{P}(D_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}) is smooth, and Proposition D.7 shows that the projectivized parametrization is finite and birational.

Let p∈ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\in\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}) and write A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top}, V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}. If kk and vv are not proportional, the fiber contains the two distinct projective points obtained by exchanging kk and vv. If they are proportional, the fiber is a singleton, but Lemma D.3 gives a dd-dimensional affine kernel. Thus pp is singular.

Conversely, if p∉ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\notin\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}), then rank⁡(V)>1\operatorname{rank}(V)>1. The projective fiber is a singleton and the affine kernel of the differential is only the scaling direction. Hence pp is smooth, and Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳1ℂ))=ℙ⁡(Zℂ).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}). ∎

The work of (Henry et al., 2025) characterizes the nontrivial fibers and critical points of the attention parametrization, which account for two possible sources of singularities. When a<da<d, there is an additional source: the parameter space DaℂD_{a}^{\mathbb{C}} is itself singular, with Sing⁡(Daℂ)=Da−1ℂ.\operatorname{Sing}(D_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})=D_{a-1}^{\mathbb{C}}. Together with the fiber and differential analysis above, this gives the singular-locus description in Lemma D.6.

For 1<a<d1<a<d, the corresponding real singular locus is 𝒳a−1\mathcal{X}_{a-1}, while for a=da=d it is contained in 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}. Thus, in both cases, the absence of proximity bias toward the real singular locus follows from Theorem 4.1. When a=1a=1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1, the nonzero real singular locus is the real counterpart ZZ of ZℂZ^{\mathbb{C}}; the absence of proximity bias toward this locus is proved next.

D.3 The rank-one model with d′>1d^{\prime}>1

See 4.2

Proof of Proposition 4.2.

Since a=1a=1, the projective determinantal variety ℙ⁡(D1ℂ)\mathbb{P}(D_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}) is smooth, and hence so is the source of the projectivized parametrization. Proposition D.7 shows that the projectivized parametrization is finite and birational.

Let p∈ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\in\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}) and write A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top}, V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}. If kk and vv are not proportional, the fiber contains the two distinct projective points obtained by exchanging kk and vv. If they are proportional, the fiber is a singleton, but Lemma D.3 gives a dd-dimensional affine kernel. Since d>1d>1, the projective differential is therefore not injective. Thus pp is singular by Lemma D.8.

Conversely, if p∉ℙ⁡(Zℂ)p\notin\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}), then rank⁡(V)>1\operatorname{rank}(V)>1. The projective fiber is a singleton and the affine kernel of the differential is only the scaling direction, so the projective differential is injective. Hence pp is smooth, and Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳1ℂ))=ℙ⁡(Zℂ).\operatorname{Sing}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}))=\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}).

We now return to the real model. Let ZZ denote the real counterpart of ZℂZ^{\mathbb{C}} and retain the locus YY defined in Equation 1. For any real preimage (A,V)(A,V) of pp, the image of the differential restricted to TD1​(A)×ℝd′×dT_{D_{1}}(A)\times\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d} is contained in T𝒳1​(p)T_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p). Consequently,

N𝒳1​(p)⊆im⁡(d​ϕ|TD1​(A)×ℝd′×d)⟂.N_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p)\subseteq\operatorname{im}\left(d\phi|_{T_{D_{1}}(A)\times\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d}}\right)^{\perp}.

At a point p∈Z∖Yp\in Z\setminus Y, choose a parametrization with A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top} and V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}, where vv is not proportional to kk. The tangent space of D1D_{1} at AA has dimension 2​d−12d-1, and the restricted differential has only the one-dimensional scaling kernel. Its image therefore has dimension 2​d+d​d′−2=dim𝒳12d+dd^{\prime}-2=\dim\mathcal{X}_{1}. Since dimZ=3​d+d′−3\dim Z=3d+d^{\prime}-3,

dim(⋃p∈Z∖Y(p+N𝒳1​(p)))\displaystyle\dim\left(\bigcup_{p\in Z\setminus Y}(p+N_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p))\right) ≤3​d+d′−3+n−(2​d+d​d′−2)=n−(d−1)​(d′−1)<n.\displaystyle\leq 3d+d^{\prime}-3+n-(2d+dd^{\prime}-2)=n-(d-1)(d^{\prime}-1)<n.

For p∈Yp\in Y, the dd-dimensional kernel from Lemma D.3 lies in TD1​(A)×ℝd′×dT_{D_{1}}(A)\times\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}\times d}. Hence the restricted differential has rank d+d​d′−1d+dd^{\prime}-1. Since dimY≤d′+2​d−2\dim Y\leq d^{\prime}+2d-2,

dim(⋃p∈Y(p+N𝒳1​(p)))\displaystyle\dim\left(\bigcup_{p\in Y}(p+N_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p))\right) ≤d′+2​d−2+n−(d+d​d′−1)=n−(d−1)​(d′−1)<n.\displaystyle\leq d^{\prime}+2d-2+n-(d+dd^{\prime}-1)=n-(d-1)(d^{\prime}-1)<n.

Finally, since 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} is a symmetric cone, we get N𝒳1​(0)=span⁡(𝒳1)⟂,N_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(0)=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{X}_{1})^{\perp}, which is a proper linear subspace. Thus the union of the translated normal cones over the real singular locus is not full-dimensional, so there is no proximity bias toward the real singular locus. ∎

D.4 The scalar-output rank-one model

When d′=1d^{\prime}=1, the dimension-counting argument of the previous subsection no longer rules out proximity bias: the upper bounds there become n−(d−1)​(d′−1)=nn-(d-1)(d^{\prime}-1)=n. Moreover, in this case the parametrization is generically two-to-one due to the symmetry exchanging kk and vv, and at the locus where kk and vv are proportional its differential has a dd-dimensional kernel. Thus these parameters do not give local coordinates on the model at the points of interest. We therefore introduce an injective parametrization that removes this symmetry. Write

ψ⁡(q,S)​(X)=(∑j=1txj⊤​S​xj)​q⊤​X,\psi(q,S)(X)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{t}x_{j}^{\top}Sx_{j}\right)q^{\top}X,

and define U={ψ(q,S):q∈ℝd,rank(S)≤1}U=\{\psi(q,S):q\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 1\} and Uℂ={ψ(q,S):q∈ℂd,rank(S)≤1}U^{\mathbb{C}}=\{\psi(q,S):q\in\mathbb{C}^{d},\ \operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 1\}.

See 4.3

Figure 4 illustrates the two geometric regimes in the smallest cases d=2d=2 and d=3d=3. As shown in Lemma D.9, the map q⊗S↦ψ⁡(q,S)q\otimes S\mapsto\psi(q,S) is injective for t>1t>1, so these low-dimensional slices faithfully represent the corresponding geometry of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1}. For d=2d=2, the locus UU lies on the boundary of the real model despite the algebraic model being smooth, whereas for d=3d=3 it appears as a singular locus.

Lemma D.9.

Suppose that a=d′=1a=d^{\prime}=1. Write A=k​q⊤A=kq^{\top}, V=v⊤V=v^{\top}, and set S=(v​k⊤+k​v⊤)/2S=(vk^{\top}+kv^{\top})/2. Then ϕ⁡(A,V)=ψ⁡(q,S)\phi(A,V)=\psi(q,S).

For 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}, the map q⊗S↦ψ⁡(q,S)q\otimes S\mapsto\psi(q,S) is an injective linear map from 𝔽d⊗S2​(𝔽d)\mathbb{F}^{d}\otimes S^{2}(\mathbb{F}^{d}) into the ambient function space. Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, the matrices SS arising in this way are exactly the symmetric matrices of rank at most two. Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, they are exactly the symmetric matrices having at most one positive and at most one negative eigenvalue.

Proof.

The formula for ϕ\phi follows from v⊤​X​X⊤​k=∑j(v⊤​xj)​(k⊤​xj)v^{\top}XX^{\top}k=\sum_{j}(v^{\top}x_{j})(k^{\top}x_{j}).

For injectivity, consider two distinct tokens. In the output coordinate corresponding to the first token, the terms linear in x1x_{1} and quadratic in x2x_{2} are (q⊤​x1)​(x2⊤​S​x2)(q^{\top}x_{1})(x_{2}^{\top}Sx_{2}), whose coefficients recover q⊗Sq\otimes S.

Clearly rank⁡(S)≤2\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2. Conversely, over ℂ\mathbb{C}, every symmetric matrix of rank at most two can be written as S=u​u⊤+w​w⊤S=uu^{\top}+ww^{\top}. Taking v=u+i​wv=u+iw and k=u−i​wk=u-iw gives S=(v​k⊤+k​v⊤)/2S=(vk^{\top}+kv^{\top})/2.

Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, set p=(v+k)/2p=(v+k)/2 and r=(v−k)/2r=(v-k)/2. Then S=p​p⊤−r​r⊤S=pp^{\top}-rr^{\top}, so SS has at most one positive and at most one negative eigenvalue. Conversely, every symmetric matrix with this property can be written as p​p⊤−r​r⊤pp^{\top}-rr^{\top}, and hence arises from v=p+rv=p+r and k=p−rk=p-r. ∎

Set 𝒟2sym={S∈S2​(ℂd):rank⁡(S)≤2}.\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}=\{S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{d}):\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2\}. By Lemma D.9, ℙ⁡(𝒳1ℂ)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}) is linearly isomorphic to the Segre embedding of ℙd−1×ℙ⁡(𝒟2sym)\mathbb{P}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}).

Lemma D.10.

If d>2d>2, then the singular locus of ℙ⁡(𝒟2sym)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}) is its rank-one locus. If d=2d=2, ℙ⁡(𝒟2sym)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}) is smooth.

Proof.

If d=2d=2, every symmetric matrix has rank at most two, so 𝒟2sym=S2​(ℂ2)\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}=S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{2}). Suppose that d>2d>2. At a rank-two matrix SS, choose coordinates with S=(S0000)S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}S_{0}&0\\ 0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right), where S0S_{0} is invertible. A nearby symmetric matrix can be written as (PQQ⊤R)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}P&Q\\ Q^{\top}&R\end{smallmatrix}\right). Since PP remains invertible, the rank-at-most-two condition is locally equivalent to R=Q⊤​P−1​QR=Q^{\top}P^{-1}Q. Hence the variety is smooth at SS. The variety is defined by its 3×33\times 3 minors. At a matrix of rank at most one, the differential of every such minor vanishes, since every partial derivative is a 2×22\times 2 minor. Thus the Zariski tangent space is the full ambient space. Since 𝒟2sym\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}} is proper for d>2d>2, every projective rank-one point is singular. ∎

We now return to the real model. Let

ℛ1={S∈S2​(ℝd):S​ has at most one positive and at most one negative eigenvalue}.\mathcal{R}_{1}=\{S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):S\text{ has at most one positive and at most one negative eigenvalue}\}.

By Lemma D.9, 𝒳1={ψ(q,S):q∈ℝd,S∈ℛ1}\mathcal{X}_{1}=\{\psi(q,S):q\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ S\in\mathcal{R}_{1}\}.

Lemma D.11.

Let S∈ℛ1S\in\mathcal{R}_{1} be positive semidefinite of rank one and K=ker⁡(S)K=\ker(S), so dimK=d−1\dim K=d-1. Since K⟂K^{\perp} is one-dimensional, with respect to ℝd=K⟂⊕K\mathbb{R}^{d}=K^{\perp}\oplus K write

Proposition D.12.

The union of the Voronoi cells of points in UU contains a nonempty open subset of the ambient space; that is, int⁡(⋃p∈UVor𝒳1⁡(p))≠∅.\operatorname{int}\left(\bigcup_{p\in U}\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p)\right)\neq\varnothing. Hence there is proximity bias toward UU.

S′=(PQQ⊤R).S^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}P&Q\\ Q^{\top}&R\end{pmatrix}.

for some c0>0c_{0}>0. ‖x−(p+w)‖2−‖p−(p+w)‖2\displaystyle\|x-(p+w)\|^{2}-\|p-(p+w)\|^{2} =‖x−p‖2−2​⟨w,x−p⟩>0.\displaystyle=\|x-p\|^{2}-2\langle w,x-p\rangle>0.

codimX~⁡(U)=(d+12)−d=(d2)=dimS2​(K).\operatorname{codim}_{\widetilde{X}}(U)=\binom{d+1}{2}-d=\binom{d}{2}=\dim S^{2}(K).

The map W↦wWW\mapsto w_{W} is injective and tangent directions to UU have zero K×KK\times K block, so wW∈TU​(p)⟂∩TX~​(p).w_{W}\in T_{U}(p)^{\perp}\cap T_{\widetilde{X}}(p). The dimension equality above therefore implies that, as WW varies, the vectors wWw_{W} fill TU​(p)⟂∩TX~​(p).T_{U}(p)^{\perp}\cap T_{\widetilde{X}}(p). Allowing η∈TX~​(p)⟂\eta\in T_{\widetilde{X}}(p)^{\perp} gives all of TU​(p)⟂T_{U}(p)^{\perp}.

Since the condition W|K≻0W|_{K}\succ 0 is open, the preceding construction gives an open subset of the normal bundle of U∖{0}U\setminus\{0\} consisting of sufficiently small vectors ww such that p+w∈Vor𝒳1⁡(p).p+w\in\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p). Consider the addition map Θ⁡(p,w)=p+w.\Theta(p,w)=p+w. Along the zero section, d​Θ(p,0)​(v,ξ)=v+ξ,d\Theta_{(p,0)}(v,\xi)=v+\xi, which is an isomorphism since TU​(p)⊕TU​(p)⟂T_{U}(p)\oplus T_{U}(p)^{\perp} is the ambient space. Hence d​Θd\Theta remains invertible at sufficiently small admissible nonzero vectors. By the inverse function theorem, the image of these vectors contains a nonempty open subset of the ambient space. Since every point in this image belongs to Vor𝒳1⁡(p)\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p) for some p∈Up\in U, we obtain int⁡(⋃p∈UVor𝒳1⁡(p))≠∅.\operatorname{int}\left(\bigcup_{p\in U}\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(p)\right)\neq\varnothing. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.3.

By Lemma D.9, ℙ⁡(𝒳1ℂ)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}) is linearly isomorphic to the Segre embedding of ℙd−1×ℙ⁡(𝒟2sym)\mathbb{P}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}). If d>2d>2, Lemma D.10 shows that the singular locus is exactly the image of the rank-one locus in 𝒟2sym\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}, namely ℙ⁡(Uℂ)\mathbb{P}(U^{\mathbb{C}}). If d=2d=2, then 𝒟2sym=S2​(ℂ2)\mathcal{D}_{2}^{\mathrm{sym}}=S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{2}), so ℙ⁡(𝒳1ℂ)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{1}^{\mathbb{C}}) is smooth.

Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, the model is parametrized by S∈ℛ1S\in\mathcal{R}_{1}. At every positive semidefinite rank-one matrix, Lemma D.11 gives a nontrivial one-sided normal cone, so these points lie on the boundary of the real model. Replacing SS by −S-S gives the same conclusion for the negative semidefinite rank-one matrices. Thus the nonzero locus UU is a boundary of the real model. Finally, Proposition D.12 gives proximity bias toward UU. ∎

Throughout this section, assume that t=1t=1. Writing S=12​(A+A⊤)S=\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{\top}), the attention map takes the form ψ⁡(S,V)​(x)=(V​x)​(x⊤​S​x).\psi(S,V)(x)=(Vx)(x^{\top}Sx).

E.1 Factorization singularities

The main difference from the multiple-token case is that the relevant factor is now the quadratic form QS​(x)=x⊤​S​xQ_{S}(x)=x^{\top}Sx.

Lemma E.1.

Let S∈S2​(ℂd)S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{d}). The quadratic form QSQ_{S} is reducible if and only if rank⁡(S)≤2\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2.

Every nonzero projective fiber of ψ\psi is finite. Moreover, the projective fiber is a singleton unless rank⁡(V)=1\operatorname{rank}(V)=1 and rank⁡(S)≤2\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2. If V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}, the differential drops rank precisely when v⊤​xv^{\top}x divides QS​(x)Q_{S}(x). In that case the affine kernel has dimension dd; otherwise it consists only of the scaling direction.

Proof.

A quadratic form over ℂ\mathbb{C} factors into two linear forms precisely when its symmetric matrix has rank at most two. Now suppose ψ⁡(S,V)=ψ⁡(S′,V′)≠0.\psi(S,V)=\psi(S^{\prime},V^{\prime})\neq 0. If rank⁡(V)>1\operatorname{rank}(V)>1, two nonproportional rows of VV, together with unique factorization, determine QSQ_{S} and hence (S,V)(S,V) up to scaling. If rank⁡(V)=1\operatorname{rank}(V)=1, write V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top}. When QSQ_{S} is irreducible, unique factorization again gives only the scaling ambiguity. Thus nontrivial fibers can occur only when rank⁡(V)=1\operatorname{rank}(V)=1 and rank⁡(S)≤2\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2. When rank⁡(V)=1\operatorname{rank}(V)=1 and QSQ_{S} is reducible, unique factorization shows that any other preimage is obtained by assigning one of the finitely many linear factors of (v⊤​x)​QS​(x)(v^{\top}x)Q_{S}(x) to V′V^{\prime}, so the projective fiber is finite.

For the differential, write v˙i⊤\dot{v}_{i}^{\top} for the rows of V˙\dot{V}. The kernel equation is

(v˙i⊤​x)​QS​(x)+(vi⊤​x)​QB​(x)=0.(\dot{v}_{i}^{\top}x)Q_{S}(x)+(v_{i}^{\top}x)Q_{B}(x)=0.

The same factorization argument gives only the scaling direction unless V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top} and v⊤​xv^{\top}x divides QS​(x)Q_{S}(x). In the latter case, writing QS​(x)=(v⊤​x)​(w⊤​x)Q_{S}(x)=(v^{\top}x)(w^{\top}x), the kernel is parametrized by r∈ℂdr\in\mathbb{C}^{d} through V˙=h​r⊤\dot{V}=hr^{\top} and QB​(x)=−(r⊤​x)​(w⊤​x),Q_{B}(x)=-(r^{\top}x)(w^{\top}x), and therefore has dimension dd. ∎

Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, let Zℂ={ψ(S,V):rank(V)=1,rank(S)≤2}Z^{\mathbb{C}}=\{\psi(S,V):\operatorname{rank}(V)=1,\ \operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2\}, and let ZZ denote the corresponding locus over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proposition E.2.

Assume that a=d>1a=d>1 and d′>1d^{\prime}>1. Then Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳dℂ))=ℙ⁡(Zℂ)\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{d}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}) and there is no proximity bias toward the corresponding real singular locus ZZ.

Proof.

By Lemma E.1, the projectivized parametrization has finite fibers and is generically one-to-one. Since its source is smooth, the finite-birational criterion from Lemma D.8 shows that the singular points are exactly those in ℙ⁡(Zℂ)\mathbb{P}(Z^{\mathbb{C}}): outside ZℂZ^{\mathbb{C}} the fiber is a singleton and the projective differential is injective, whereas on ZℂZ^{\mathbb{C}} there is either a nontrivial fiber or a critical preimage.

We now work over ℝ\mathbb{R}. For p∈𝒳dp\in\mathcal{X}_{d}, set ℒp=p+⋂(S,V)∈ψ−1​(p)im⁡(d​ψ(S,V))⟂\mathcal{L}_{p}=p+\bigcap_{(S,V)\in\psi^{-1}(p)}\operatorname{im}(d\psi_{(S,V)})^{\perp}. Since every image of the differential is contained in T𝒳d​(p)T_{\mathcal{X}_{d}}(p), we have Vor𝒳dloc⁡(p)⊆p+N𝒳d​(p)⊆ℒp\operatorname{Vor}^{\operatorname{loc}}_{\mathcal{X}_{d}}(p)\subseteq p+N_{\mathcal{X}_{d}}(p)\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{p}.

To bound ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} over the real singular locus ZZ, we separate the exceptional locus Y={ψ(v⊗2,hv⊤):v≠0,h≠0}⊆ZY=\{\psi(v^{\otimes 2},hv^{\top}):v\neq 0,\ h\neq 0\}\subseteq Z. For points in Z∖YZ\setminus Y, there is always a noncritical preimage, which gives the stronger dimension bound below. On YY, the unique projective preimage is critical, so a separate bound is needed.

Set n=d′​(d+23)n=d^{\prime}\binom{d+2}{3} and m=d​d′+(d+12)m=dd^{\prime}+\binom{d+1}{2}, so that dim𝒳d=m−1\dim\mathcal{X}_{d}=m-1.

Let p∈Z∖(Y∪{0})p\in Z\setminus(Y\cup\{0\}). If pp already has a noncritical preimage, there is nothing to show. Otherwise, choose a critical preimage (S,V)(S,V). By Lemma E.1, we may write V=h​v⊤V=hv^{\top} and QS​(x)=(v⊤​x)​(w⊤​x)Q_{S}(x)=(v^{\top}x)(w^{\top}x). Since p∉Yp\notin Y, we have w|vw\not\parallel v. The same output then has a parametrization with V′=h​w⊤V^{\prime}=hw^{\top} and QS′​(x)=(v⊤​x)2Q_{S^{\prime}}(x)=(v^{\top}x)^{2}, which is noncritical. Hence dimℒp≤n−(m−1)\dim\mathcal{L}_{p}\leq n-(m-1). Since dimZ≤d′+3​d−3\dim Z\leq d^{\prime}+3d-3,

dim(⋃p∈Z∖(Y∪{0})ℒp)≤n−(d−1)​(2​d′+d−4)2<n.\dim\left(\bigcup_{p\in Z\setminus(Y\cup\{0\})}\mathcal{L}_{p}\right)\leq n-\frac{(d-1)(2d^{\prime}+d-4)}{2}<n.

For p∈Yp\in Y, the projective preimage is unique and Lemma E.1 gives a dd-dimensional affine kernel. Thus dimℒp=n−(m−d)\dim\mathcal{L}_{p}=n-(m-d). Since dimY=d′+d−1\dim Y=d^{\prime}+d-1,

dim(⋃p∈Yℒp)≤n−(d−1)​(2​d′+d−2)2<n.\dim\left(\bigcup_{p\in Y}\mathcal{L}_{p}\right)\leq n-\frac{(d-1)(2d^{\prime}+d-2)}{2}<n.

Finally, since 𝒳d\mathcal{X}_{d} is a symmetric cone, its local Voronoi cell at the origin is contained in a proper linear subspace. Hence the union of the local Voronoi cells over ZZ has empty interior. ∎

E.2 Rank-constrained models

The second new feature in the regime t=1t=1 is that symmetrization interacts differently with the rank constraint over ℂ\mathbb{C} and over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proposition E.3.

Let 1≤a<d1\leq a<d and let S=12​(A+A⊤)S=\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{\top}). Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, the possible symmetric parts of matrices satisfying rank⁡(A)≤a\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq a are exactly {S∈S2​(ℂd):rank⁡(S)≤min⁡{2​a,d}}\{S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{d}):\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq\min\{2a,d\}\}. Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, they are exactly ℛa={S∈S2(ℝd):n+(S)≤a,n−(S)≤a}\mathcal{R}_{a}=\{S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):n_{+}(S)\leq a,\ n_{-}(S)\leq a\}, where n+​(S)n_{+}(S) and n−​(S)n_{-}(S) denote the numbers of positive and negative eigenvalues of SS, respectively.

Proof.

The inclusion rank⁡(S)≤2​a\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2a over ℂ\mathbb{C} is immediate. Conversely, write S=∑i=1rui​ui⊤S=\sum_{i=1}^{r}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top} with r≤2​ar\leq 2a. Pairing the summands and using Sym⁡((u+i​v)​(u−i​v)⊤)=u​u⊤+v​v⊤\operatorname{Sym}((u+iv)(u-iv)^{\top})=uu^{\top}+vv^{\top} expresses SS as the symmetric part of a sum of at most ⌈r/2⌉≤a\lceil r/2\rceil\leq a rank-one matrices.

Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, if A=K⊤​QA=K^{\top}Q with K,Q∈ℝa×dK,Q\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times d}, then Sym⁡(A)=P​P⊤−R​R⊤\operatorname{Sym}(A)=PP^{\top}-RR^{\top} for suitable P,R∈ℝd×aP,R\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times a}, so it has at most aa positive and at most aa negative eigenvalues. The converse follows by reversing this construction. ∎

If 2​a≥d2a\geq d, the complexified model is therefore the same as in the unconstrained case. The genuinely new regime is 2​a<d2a<d.

Proposition E.4.

Assume that a>1a>1 and 2​a<d2a<d. Then Sing⁡(ℙ⁡(𝒳aℂ))=ℙ⁡({ψ⁡(S,V):rank⁡(S)≤2​a−1}).\operatorname{Sing}\bigl(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{X}_{a}^{\mathbb{C}})\bigr)=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\psi(S,V):\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2a-1\}\bigr).

Proof.

Proposition E.3 implies that the complex parameter space for SS is the symmetric determinantal variety 𝒟2​a={S∈S2​(ℂd):rank⁡(S)≤2​a}\mathcal{D}_{2a}=\{S\in S^{2}(\mathbb{C}^{d}):\operatorname{rank}(S)\leq 2a\}, whose singular locus is 𝒟2​a−1\mathcal{D}_{2a-1}.

Outside 𝒟2​a−1\mathcal{D}_{2a-1}, the matrix SS has rank 2​a>22a>2, so QSQ_{S} is irreducible. Hence the projective fiber is a singleton and the projective differential is injective. By Lemma E.1, the projectivized parametrization has finite fibers and is generically one-to-one, hence is finite and birational. The finite-birational criterion D.8 therefore gives smoothness there. Conversely, every point in the displayed locus has a preimage in the singular locus 𝒟2​a−1\mathcal{D}_{2a-1} of the parameter space, and is therefore singular. ∎

Let UU be the locus of points ψ⁡(S,V)\psi(S,V) with V≠0V\neq 0 and inertia⁡(S)=(a,a−1,d−2​a+1)\operatorname{inertia}(S)=(a,a-1,d-2a+1). Since ψ⁡(S,V)=ψ⁡(−S,−V)\psi(S,V)=\psi(-S,-V), inertia (a−1,a,d−2​a+1)(a-1,a,d-2a+1) gives the same set.

Lemma E.5.

Let S∈ℛaS\in\mathcal{R}_{a} have inertia (a,a−1,k)(a,a-1,k), where k=d−2​a+1k=d-2a+1, and let K=ker⁡(S)K=\ker(S). With respect to ℝd=K⟂⊕K\mathbb{R}^{d}=K^{\perp}\oplus K, write S=(S0000)S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}S_{0}&0\\ 0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right), and let B22B_{22} denote the K×KK\times K block of BB. Then

Tℛa(S)={B:B22⪯0,rank(B22)≤1},Nℛa(S)={W:W=PKWPK,W|K⪰0}.T_{\mathcal{R}_{a}}(S)=\{B:B_{22}\preceq 0,\ \operatorname{rank}(B_{22})\leq 1\},\qquad N_{\mathcal{R}_{a}}(S)=\{W:W=P_{K}WP_{K},\ W|_{K}\succeq 0\}.

For inertia (a−1,a,k)(a-1,a,k), the inequalities are reversed.

Proof.

For a nearby matrix S′=(PQQ⊤R)S^{\prime}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}P&Q\\ Q^{\top}&R\end{smallmatrix}\right), the block PP has inertia (a,a−1)(a,a-1). Hence the inertia constraint on S′S^{\prime} is, to first order, equivalent to requiring the Schur complement R−Q⊤​P−1​QR-Q^{\top}P^{-1}Q to be negative semidefinite of rank at most one. Conversely, if B22⪯0B_{22}\preceq 0 and rank⁡(B22)≤1\operatorname{rank}(B_{22})\leq 1, choosing a curve whose Schur complement is t​B22tB_{22} realizes BB as a tangent direction. Taking the polar gives the normal cone. The other case follows by replacing SS by −S-S. ∎

Proposition E.6.

Assume that a>1a>1 and 2​a<d2a<d. There is proximity bias toward UU.

Proof.

The argument is the same normal-bundle argument used in Proposition D.12.

Fix p=ψ⁡(S,V)∈Up=\psi(S,V)\in U and let K=ker⁡(S)K=\ker(S). Since rank⁡(S)=2​a−1>2\operatorname{rank}(S)=2a-1>2, the unrestricted symmetric parametrization is, after quotienting by scaling, a local diffeomorphism near pp. Choose WW supported on KK with W|K≻0W|_{K}\succ 0, and transport it through this local parametrization to a normal direction wWw_{W} at pp. By Lemma E.5 and the Schur complement, for x∈𝒳ax\in\mathcal{X}_{a} sufficiently close to pp we have ⟨wW,x−p⟩≤c​‖x−p‖2\langle w_{W},x-p\rangle\leq c\|x-p\|^{2}. Writing k=d−2​a+1k=d-2a+1, the admissible matrices WW form an open subset of S2​(K)S^{2}(K), and dimS2​(K)=(k+12)=codim𝒳d⁡(U)\dim S^{2}(K)=\binom{k+1}{2}=\operatorname{codim}_{\mathcal{X}_{d}}(U). Together with the directions normal to 𝒳d\mathcal{X}_{d}, these directions fill TU​(p)⟂T_{U}(p)^{\perp}. The inverse-function-theorem argument from Proposition D.12 therefore shows that ⋃p∈UVor𝒳a⁡(p)\bigcup_{p\in U}\operatorname{Vor}_{\mathcal{X}_{a}}(p) contains a nonempty open subset of the ambient space. ∎

Appendix F Numerical evidence for Conjecture 3.16

Let n=dimℋn=\dim\mathcal{H}. For f∈ℱ′f\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, let m⁡(f)m(f) be the dimension of the span of im⁡d​Φθ\operatorname{im}d\Phi_{\theta} over all parameters θ\theta of the full network with fθ=ff_{\theta}=f, where Φ:θ↦fθ\Phi:\theta\mapsto f_{\theta} is the parametrization of ℱ\mathcal{F}. The normal cone Nℱ​(f)N_{\mathcal{F}}(f) lies in a space of dimension n−m⁡(f)n-m(f), by Remark 3.8. So there is no proximity bias toward ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} if m⁡(f)m(f) exceeds the dimension of every subset of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} on which it is constant, by Lemma B.8. At a generic point of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, this means m⁡(f)>dimℱ′m(f)>\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

We computed m⁡(f)m(f) at random parameters, with exact linear algebra modulo a large prime. To explore the fiber of ff, we gave the inactive neurons random incoming weights and merged constant or proportional neurons into the next layer.

We tested 10,768 networks with bias terms: d0≤2d_{0}\leq 2, L∈{3,4}L\in\{3,4\}, hidden widths at most 33, dL≤2d_{L}\leq 2, activations t2t^{2}, t3t^{3} or generic quadratics and cubics, and one or two inactive neurons.

inactive neurons cases dimℱ′<dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\dim\mathcal{F} with m>dimℱ′m>\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}
one, in one layer 5088 2884 2884
two, in one layer 2544 2148 2148
one in each of two layers 3136 2666 2666

The condition holds in all 7,698 cases with dimℱ′<dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}<\dim\mathcal{F}. In the 3,070 cases with dimℱ′=dimℱ\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{F}, where there is proximity bias by Proposition 2.4, we found m=dimℱ′m=\dim\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

We also tested 40,000 degenerate subsets of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, taken from 1,600 of these cases. They are defined by zero weights, inactive or dead neurons, equal, opposite or proportional neurons, or zero biases. The condition holds on all of them, except those consisting of constant functions, where Nℱ={0}N_{\mathcal{F}}=\{0\} because of the output bias.

The ranks are exact with high probability but not certified, and only some degenerate subsets were tested. They provide evidence for the conjecture. For a fixed small architecture, an exact symbolic computation of the strata of ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} on which m⁡(f)m(f) is constant would give a proof.
